A PROBLEII SOLVED. Sandy and Ned were brothers, Ned was older than Sandy; And they were busy dividing A stick of peppermint candy. Ned was earnestly trying To make the division true, And he marked the place with a fishhook, Where the stick ought to break in two. But, alas, for little Sandy And his poor painstaking brother! 'Twas a long and a short division— One piece longer than the other. Ned gravely looked at the pieces And their quite unequal length, And he wrestled with the problem With all his mental strength. And at last he 2ald—" Oh, Sandy! I can make It wale out right, Ti I take the piece that's longest, And bite off just one bite." Their four eyes beamed and brightened At this plan, so very handy, Of diipoiing of the problem And distributing the candy. So Ned ate the pieces even— 'Twas the simplest way to do it; And he cheated little Sandy— And they neither of them knew it
Varittico.

"When I tell this story in France," pleasantly added the narrator, " I make the Englishman go up the chimney." At the celebratio-n of the birthday of a neighbouring gen- tleman, the minister, on the hospitable entertainer pro- posing a bumper to the health of the King, testified his loyalty by joining in the demonstration of it, but stated his hope that such a toast should not be very frequently re- peat,d, "for," adds he, "if you drink many such bumpsrs to the health of the King, you will assuredly injure the consti- tution. Sir C. 8- being at an inn on the road, a report came that a 4entleman had been robbed, on which he swore "that a single highwayman should not rot) him." The next morn- ing, going on his journey, one met him and repeated the very words Sir C- had made use of the night before. "But there are two of you," replied Sir C-. The man, surprised by the impromptu, suddenly turned his head round to look for hie comrade, when Sir C- instanCy shot him dead.

A well-known lawyer, who is fond of fishing, sent a telegram to the innkeeper at a favourite resort of anglers, requesting the usual preparations to be made for him, in the shape of dinner, bed, dr...1. On reaching his destina- tion the next day, he was surprised to find his arrival un- expected, and nothing really as he had desired. "Did you not get my message ? " he asked, in astonishment. "Oh, yea, we got a letter, hnl., as it was not in your own handwriting, we paid no attention to It!" said the honest Innkeeper. In a certain cemetery is a curious trio of graves—those of a man and his two wives. On the gravestone to the right was a:m.7st' a hand pointing to the centre, with the Inscrip- tion—" He was mine." The stone to the left had also a hand directed towards the middle mound, with the words— "He was mine also." In the middle lay the remains of the "lord" himself, and upon the headstone were carved two hands, reaching in either direction as if to clasp the other two. Above them were the significant words—" They were both mine."

THE SAVING OF THE SCOTTISH REGALIA.—The siege of Dunottar was converted into a blockade in the beginning of May, 1652, and the service was entrusted to Colonel Thos. Morgan, who had with him Monk's Regiment (now the Coldstream Guards), some horse, dragoons, and a train of guns. The latter he got into position for bombarding the place, while he encamped at the Black Hill of Danottar, and, ere long, the garrison became reduced to the greatest straits by the want of provisions. Toe besiegers looked upon the capture of the Scottish regalia as of more im- portance than of the castle, and Colonel Mackinnon says, tha% "Monk's own regiment was probably selected for this gisrVice that it might have the credit of the capture of the Flunenrs of Scotland,' it being well known that the regalia was deoosited for safety in this castle." However, they ware happily never fated to fell into republican hands, for they were saved by the ingenuity, bravery, and patriotism of a woman, with the connivance of the governor, who agreed that he was to be kept ignorant of the place of their concealmeet, lest the English, by torture, might wring the secret from him. Armed by a par,. from Colonel Morgan, the wife of Mr. James Grainger, minister of the aolotuios parish of Kineff, accompanied by her maidservant, bearing on her back a quantity of flex, which she pretended she had botuhc at Stonehaven, was permitted to visit the governor's lady. She rode on horseback, as if she had come from that town, and left the animal at the gate while she and the girl were in the fortress. Unknown to the governor, hi dy packed up the sword of state and the sceptre in the Ica bag of flex, while Mrs. Grainger brought out the royal crown in her lap! When leaving the castle, she was cour- teously assisted to her saddle by Colonel Morgan in person. The lady and her servant passed safely through the Eng- lish camp with those royal insignia, in defence of which perhaps a million of Scotsmen have died in battle, and that night saw them safely under the floor of the parish church, where they lay till the Restoration, and, strange to say, quite unipjured, as their unknown guardians frequently re- newed the linen in which they were wrapped.—" British Battles an Land and Sea."

A greater number of sheep than these might have been grazed on the plot, as some of the grass was cut for hay, it being more than the sheep could consume. The pasture is composed of cow grass, red clover, and rye-grass, and the seed having only been sown in August, 1881, the pasture is not yet at its best, and will be much better in a year or two, while the land will be permanently enriched to a state of fertility hitherto unknown in pasture razing. [Publishecl &it 3f P T Ir;bbieiehite, 31. Tavistocic-strer London, fr.C., and reprtnted by pernusszon.J THE WALPOLES. The County of Norfolk has furnished to the country an I unusually large proportion of able and successful pulilic ' men— the Townshends, Nelsons, Cokes, De Greys, and many others. Among them the name of Walpole will take no mean place. The Earl of Orford, the present head of the• house, owns 12,341 acres of land in Norfolk, with a rent-roll of £15,313. The Walpoles claim to have been settled in the county prior to the Norman Conquest; and it is certain ' that, not long after that event, they held lands of the Bishopric of Ely, at the place from whence they derive their I surname. Somewhat later they acquired the manor of Houghton, which was for a lengthened period the seat of the family, and at which place Sir Robert Walpole erected a magnificent mansion. In the reign of Elizabeth the heir of ' the Walpoles was indicted for treason; but his forfeited lands were granted to his next brother, to whom his father also bequeathed his own lands at his death. The grand- , father of Sir Robert sat in the Restoration Parliament, and his father was also at one time a member of the House of Commons. It is not my province here to deal at length with Sir Robert Walpole's conduct of public affairs. Suffice it to say that, with all his faults, he was a wise and able statesman, who rendered inestimable services to his country. It cannot be denied that, if he used his opportunities to enrich himself and his family, his personal gains were but small when compared with the great increment of national prosperity which resulted from the policy which he steadfastly pursued. His memory need shrink from no comparison with his immediate predecessors or successors. I have only to do with him as an example of the fact that several of our great families have been built up by pursuing the pro- fession of politics. Sir Robert's father was a simply conntry squire of mode- rate fortune—between £2,000 and £3,000 a year. Robert, who was a younger son, was originally intended for the Church ; but, on the death of his elder brother, he was called

div.head: STATE oF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE oF IRELAND.
On Friday, a passenger in a Cork train jumped head fore- most through the window of the carriage, and was killed instantaneously. Deceased was travelling without a ticket, and tried to escape. _ _

The Gray Committee reassembled, on Tuesday, to con- sider a proposed amendment to their report. Mr. Sexton proposed to add a-paragraph declaring that the singularly anomalous law of contempt demanded the further•attention of the Hous?, but the proposal was rejected by nine rotes to three. One of the Dublin papers says that during a recent inter- view with the Bishops of Down and Achonry the Pope expr •ased his ho-ror at the crimes and outrages being com- mitted in Ireland, and charged them to exert themselves to guide the people and prevent them from offending the laws. On Monday, ten prisoners were charged, at Loughrea, with assaulting Captain Mallen, of Gort, and other gentle- men of the hunt, in the neighbourhood of Longtime. The Crown withdrew the charge under the Crimes Act, subditu- tiug the common law. The farmers have subscribed £3O for the defence. The prisoners were remanded. A farmer named Cullen was sentencel to two months' im- prisonment at Clonmel, on Saturday morning, under the Prevention of Crimes Act, for threatening a farmer named Hickey and his wife, because Hickey would not quash a bargain for the pnrehase of the interest in some land from Cullen, of which the latter had repented. A new swing bridge, erected at a cost of upwards of £30.000, and named after Mr. Parnell, member for the city of Cork, was on Saturday opened by the mayor for traffic. It was originally the intention to have the structure opened by Mr. Parnell himself, but that gentleman wrote that the state of his health was such as would prevent his presence. The well-to•do sections of the citizens were conspicuous by their absence from the opening oeremony. Lady Florence Dixie asks in God's name why the Land League are hugging their unexpended balance of £32,800, when it could be used to ward off the suffering and terrors of famine. The fund, she declares, was raised to. relieve dis- tress, and should be applied to that purpose, or "the death and misery of hundreds will lay at the door of the great Land League." The answer given to the previous question of this lady does not encourage the belief that her present inquiry will produce much effect. Tine IRISH SKIRMISHING FUND : DISAYPRARANCII OF £36,390 —The committee appointed in New York to inquire into the expenditure of the Irish Skirmishing Fund, reports that no part of the fund has been used for the purpose for which it was ints.-ae4 It was alleged that 436,390 hes been spent by applying it to uncoil,-- _ (I'K 11 used £lO,OOO to assist in the election to Parliament or Devoy, and A 5,000 was devoted to an effort to control the Dublin Irishman. The committee report their continued confidence that the skirmishing fund is the simplest and most efficient mode of making warfare against England Iwhich the Irish can adopt, and they advise 'other coun- tries where the Irish are found in large numbers to adopt similar schemes.

ANorimgc Aortiumi OUTRAGR.--Some particulars are published of an outrage reported to have been committed betweea Oldcastle and Ballyjamesduff, on the border line between Meath and Cavan. A correspondent says a respect- able farmer, named M'Enroe, of Cermeen, was returning with one of his servants from the fur of Oldeastle when he was stopped just outside the boundary bridge by some men. They asked M'Enroe if he would give up the farm formerly held by his brother. M'Enroe determinedly replied that be would not, whereupon one ef the party fired a shot from a revolver over his head. Persisting in his refusal, M'Enroe endeavoured to drive off, whereupon one of the men stepped upon the axle of his car and deliberately fired two shots at his head, one of which lodged in the head and the other in his neck. They then decamped. The servant drove home with the wounded man as fast as he was able. Medical and clerical aid was summoned, but M'Enroe remained unconscious, and no trace of the bullets has been , found.

Tun ArtsmpT TO SHOOT JUDGI LAWSON% Peter Delaney, who is in custody at Dubin, charged with at- ttempting to shoot Mr. Justice Llwsoa, was taken on Mon- day to the police court under a strong guard of mounted police with drawn sabres. At two o'clock he was charged before Mr. Curran, Q C , presiding migistrate. A cabowner, named John O'Toole, said he was at the north-east corner of Fitzwilliam-square on the evening ot the lltla instant, and

saw the prisoner moving about, and watched him. Witness bade him good evening, but he made no reply. Witness saw the judge's escort passing out of the square, and the prisoner followed them. George Darker, a retired non-com- missioned officer of the Royal Artillery, who was one of his lordship's escort, and was with M‘Dennell, the Hussar pen- sioner, said he saw M`Donnell take the revolver from the prisoner's hand. Witness helped to disarm kim, and caught the prisoner by the throat. Prisoner caught his sleeve with his teeth. M‘Donnell kept about two paces behind the pri- soner when he crossed the street towards the judge. Other evidence followed, and the prisoner was committed for trial.

TUE ARREAI4.9 QUESTION IN IRELAND.—Mr. T. A. Dick- son, M.P., with whom Mr. Gladstde is in communication on the subject of ttre Land Act, denies that he has ever pro- nounced tile Act a failure. He adds, however, that he shall "continue ta condemn the reeent changes in connection with its administration by the .appointment of valuers, a step which has alienated the confidence of the tenants of Ulster." Mr. Dickson points out that the Tyrone election, following the Royal assent to the Land Act, was fought out upon these very issues. As to the vital question of arrears, Mr. Dickson says the first few weeks after the Act passed were spent by the Chief Commissioners and lawyers in trying to explain or solve its difficult clauses, and nearly every week the Commissioners have been issuing fresh ex- planations, so that half the time allowed by the Act has been wasted, and only within the past three weeks, as diffi- culties were removed, have landlords and tenants com- menced to avail themselves of its benefits. The reports just received sty that applications are now coming in at the rate of 1,000 per day; " but if the door suddenly closes on the 30th, and processes, decrees, and evictions follow, as they will as a matter of • course in the poorer districts af to. quarter sessions in January, he is not sanguine as to the future, and still hopes the Prime Minister may be able to surmount the difficulty."

div.head: MALMIRASNA MASSACRE.
div.p: THE MALMIRASNA MASSACRE.

Myles Joyce, the third man put on trial for participation in the terrible outrage at Maamtrasna, was on -Saturday found guilty and sentenced to death. The defence offered was an alibi. One of the principal witnesses in the trials, Anthony Joyce, stated in his evidence on Saturday that the prisoner and the head of the murdered family were both his first cousins. Thomas Casey, one of the two approvers, said he first met the man Nee, one of the supposed plotters and directors of the massacre, at North Shields. The Judge would not allow the witness to answer the question of the Attorney-General asking what Nee said to him on the way to the house at Maamtrasna. In the remarks which accom- panied his passing of sentence Mr. Justice Barry spoke of the witnesses for the prosecution as "those honest, truth- telling men."

The judicial proceedings in the case came to a close sud- denly on Tuesday. The three prisoners who were of the number who actually broke in the door of the Jaycee' house and entered the place had been convicted, and counsel for the defence now said that the remaining five prisoners— Patrick Joyce, Thomas Joyce, John Casey, Martin Joyce, and Myles Casey—would withdraw their plea of not guilty, and he appealed to the Attorney General to recommena them to the merciful consideration of the Crown and also to the Judg,! to endorse the recommendation. Air. Justice Barry then sentenced the fire mEtt to death. His'Lordship, in doing so' said it was not improbable that some of them were led to the scene of the outrage unconscious of what was to happen, nor was it improbable that some of them were induced to join in the dreadful deed through th'e influence of terrorism ; but it was absolutely impossible that any jury could have made any distinction as to the guilt of the pri- soners. • "No jury capable of estimating evidence could," added the Judge, "hesitate to hold that those who remained outside in the yard whilst the scene of carnage was being enacted within were equally guilty." In all eight men lie under doom of death for participation ia this, one of the blackest crimes of the age. . _ _

div.head: A.riRtCULTUitE N L.MISETIRE. THE EFFECTS OF THE CHEMICAL WORKS AND COLLIERIES AT ST. HELENS, WIDNES, AND RUNCORN.
div.p: A.riRtCULTUitE N L.MISETIRE. THE EFFECTS OF THE CHEMICAL WORKS AND COLLIERIES AT ST. HELENS, WIDNES, AND RUNCORN.

The Assistant Commissioner appointed under the Royal Commission on Agriculture to visit the counties of Lan- cashire, Cheshire, and Northumberland, has presented his report to Parliament. The mass of information collected by Idr. Coleman is of peculiar interest, innsmuch as it illustrates the great influence the development of manufactuaing indus- tries has had upon agricultural prosperity by providing markets for produce. The result of the investigation of the Commissioner has led to the following conclusions :—" Up to the present time the farming of Lancashire has not suffered so severely as in many other parts, although there is no doubt that much money has been lost during the last few years. This ccmparative immunity from Idistress is due in a great measure to the influence of large centres of population in providing a market for perishable and bulky produce, such as milk, vegetables, and root crops, bay and straw, and above all in affording an abundant supply of manure, which enables the skilful far- mer to keep his land in a high condition of fertility, and thereby to produce abundant crops. But the influence of towns is not entirely beneficial; the attraction of higher wages draws thither the best of the workmen, and labour would be even dearer than it is but for a large influx of Lisle partly resident and partly migratory. Even with this assistance wages have risen 20 to 25 per cent in the last 20 years. This is one evil, but there is a much greater, and one that in the nature of things must increase, unless some remedy can be found. I allude to the injury to vege- tation arising from poisonous exhalations. This is most apparent in the vicinity of chemical works, such as those at Widnes, Runcorn, and St. Helens. Here, indeed, all that comes direcily under the unadulterated influence of such works is destroyed, and the effects are visible for a radius of many miles. The influence of collieries and works where smoke from sulphurous coal is burnt without being consumed is very injurious to timber, and to a lesser heat still very material extent to crops, so much se that the feeding of animals on pasture affected by smoke is impracticable and the health of breeding stock suffers. lam aware that, as regards chemical wcrks, a recent Act imposes more strin- gent regulations, and it remains to be seen what will be the effect of this legislation. Those who have suffered are not sanguine as to say material advantage, and they are unani- mous in the opinion that the affected areas should be defined, and the owners of works Made liable for compensation, accord- ing to the nature and extent of their production. The amount of damage might be the subject of arbitration, and the share falling on each manufacture might be assessed by a committee oomposed of the manufacturers themselves, acting on certain principles defined by law." It may be added that one of the earliest visits of the Com- missioner was to the Hale estates of Colonel Blackburn. They are four miles from Widnes, and in consequence of the chemical works the aspect of the country was very deplarable, vegetation being completely destroyed, though previous to the existence of the works it was well wooded. At Farnvrorth, near Widnes, Mr. Coleman was informed by a tenant farmer that, though he did not suffer much as re- gards his crops, he cannot keep stock long on the land as they would sicken, gradually pine away, and their livers would become congested. There is, however, one advantage arising from the existing of the che:nical works, for chemical waste, suck as gas lime, is given gratis, and is found of great value when applied to the land in suitable doses. A visit was paid to the Derby and Sefton farms near Liverpool, and the Commissioner would have described them as the garden of Lancashire; out for the fact that over large portions of tbe district the blasting influence of the Widnes and Runcorn chemical works has destroyed trees, and in- jured fences and herbage. He contends that it is a dis- grace to science and civilisation that these noxious vapours should be poured forth, and that the authors of such wide- spread evil should go scot free. Most serious injury has been done, which, as regards permanent vegetation, may be described as irreparable, and attempts to punish the offenders have proved abortive from the impossibility of spotting the delinquents.

THE ACTION AGAINST RUNCORN ALKALI COMPANY. Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, was engaged for a con- siderable time at Birkenhead County Court, on Tuesday, hearing counsel in the action brought by John Cronshaw on behalf of Wm. Cronshew, a minor, against the ROOM Soap and Alkali Company to recover £l2O compensation for personal injury sustained by the plaintiff whilst in the em- ploy of the defendants.—Mr. Pickford, barrister-at-10r, addressed his Honour at great length for the defence. Assuming, he said, that his Honour gave a verdict for til? plaintiff, the compensation to which the latter was entleta could not exceed £5O on account of the terms of his ehßle ment. He pointed out the discrepancies between the evidenbe of the witnesses for the plaintiff and for the defence rdgard to the wood which the plaintiff was cutting at the time of the accident. Kirkham and Kilcross both said there was no knot in the stave in the place alleged by the plain- tiff, aud this evidence, he thought, was conclusive that there was no knot in the stave. If there was no knot, then tleil • plaintiff's theory of how the accident happend was disposa .. of to a great extent, and if his Honour coupled that wil the probability that the plaintiff's fingers were cut in the way he said, that would establish in the first plao, that the saw was equal to the work, and that the accident did not happen through the sew catching.s, knot in the wood. Plaintiff said very candidly that he dia not know how the accident did happen, and he hid not established that it occurred in the way he had described., Speaking of the alleged defect in the saw, Mr. Pickford observed that a dull SAW was not a defect within the Mean' ing of the Act.—His Honour drew Mr. Pickford's attention I, to a decision which had appeared that the word defect meant 'an inherent defect.—Mr. Pickford said it was quite e0r1; ceivable the accident might have occurred throueh a chise!l or any tool not bAng in proper order, and that would not lee celled a defect in the machinery works or plant. The sr_ in this case was nothing more than a tool worked machinery, and the fact oethis net being kept properly sherPo was not a defect within the ineaeing Of the Act. Evee assuming the saw to be a tool, it might he that if it bad hee' of iinproper construction so that it would not ruu, or if 0'1(7 or three teeth had been knocked out, and bad thereby eAce,f,e an accident, that might be considered a defect within meaning of the Act. He did not say it would be. A defef he took to mean something deficient in the machinery. saw was not deficient ; it was simply not kelpt proper order, it might be, owing to the negligen' of somebody entrusted with superintendence, or somehodY who was not entrusted with superintendence. The erq way in which Ward could be said to be negligent was Ine putting a lad to work a saw when it was dull, if it sever.' dull. But Ward examined the saw, and, to the best of h's judgment, concluded that the saw was in proper working order. Thet judgment was afterwards confirmed by Kilcrossf who said the saw was sufficiently sharp to 'ee used. If there was any negligence at all it was on the part of Kilcross, vih° was entrusted with the duty of seeing that the saw 113,n sharpened, Ward being entrusted only with the superintene" ence of the way in which it was used. Kilcross was a man ordinarily engaged in manual labour, and therefore not a person for whose negligence the plaintiff could make the de- fendants liable. The defendants distinctly proved that the plaintiff was guilty of contributory negligence. If the plaie- tiff, knowing of the dulness of the saw—its dangerous stste —at a quarter to seven in the morning, chose to work it tin' til half-past three in the afternoon, he must be deemed to have taken all risk. Mr. Pickford quoted a case in suPP°rt of that view. The plaintiff had complained to Ward, but he knew that Kilcross was the proper person to whom •be should have made the complaint. Mr. Little , interposed, remarking that Ward said he had never instructed the plaintiff to go to Kilcross. Mr. Pickford said the practice was for the lad to go to Kilcross, who he knew was the peraoi entrusted with the duty of seeing that the saw was sharp. Kilcross, too, was working all the deY within 15 yards of the plaintiff, who, however, simplY Went on working without taking the trouble to say anything about the 'dangerous condition of the saw. If Ward ree fused or neglected to test the saw to see if it were dull, but said it was all right, all the more reason why the piaictel„ should have informed Kilcross, who was se near to hina• " that respect plaintiff was clearly guilty of negligert„,n`' which in a large degree was, the cause of the accident. Pickford also contended that the improper way in which the plaintiff held the staves was also contributory negligerinee. —Mr. Little, barrister-at-law, then' replied on behalf of tee 1 plaintiff, contending with regard to compensation thet the defendants having departed out of the method of remunera• ion by weekly wages to the plaintiff, and pay him by Ws work they would,have to pay the plaintiff at the same ra,te during the three years mentioned in the Act. In those ctr: cumstancos the plaintiff would be entitled to £Bl instead ea £47, as stated by the defendants. The defendants said the? were bound to employ the plaintiff during his apprentice- ship. He (Mr. Little) admitted that during the renal% ing four years of the plaintiff's apprenticeship, he inu,s be paid at a certain rate. Still he would not be as capabl and skilful in performing his work as a man with the ftP use of his hands. They had to deal with permanent injul to the lad's working capacity, besides a great amount 0 pain and injury. During the eight weeks and three dale the lad was under the care of the doctors, the defendants paid him nothing, but left him entirely without assistance of any kind. Referring to the question of the saw, Little said all the witnesses called for the defence vier" persons interested in the matter, while it was difficult to sai whether stronger evidence could be adduced on the Part nee the plaintiff. From the beginning to the end of the caTi the defendants called no witness who was able to state tvl3,ee the saw was sharpened prior to the accident. When tu..," plaintiff made the complaint about the state of the sr.; Ward ought to have called Kilcross to give his opin't n, whether the SAW was sharp or not. Ward, his wol would remember, did not give his evidence in the sa frank, unbiassed manner, in which he thought the rest 0 the witnesses did. There was a callousness and bitterness° about the way in which be spoke, which he was beund say was not manifested by the other witnesses. P contended that there was a defect in mach,eri when it was allowed to get out of proper working orde,r; and he submitted that there had been negligence on Ward part before the moining of the accident. He was ignorant' of circular saws, and ought to have called in a sawyer V]. see the saw was in proper condition. It was by his order; that the boy worked the saw, and the injury resulte' through the lad using the saw in the bad condition described. In a case of this sort, where from the beginninege to the end every advantage had certainly been taken bY defendants to try and escape the liability of an aceicleent which was as clearly the result of the negligence of tust man Ward as anything possibly could be, he must saY ° • ,ectat he could not see of what use the Employers' LiabilitY f nf could be.—His Honour said on account of the lateness the hour he would reserve his judgment until the Sth °t3. div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

BILLS OF SALE AND FAILURES. - In the week ending November 18, 1882, there were 212 bills of sale in England, a decrease of 832 over tthose of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 206, a decrease of 20. The totals for portion of year to November 18, 1882, ate :—Bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 40,209, a decrease of 4,642, the failures gazatted number 9,408, a de- crease of 831.—Stubbs' Mercantile Gazetts.

THE floßsa NAIL TRADE. At a representative meeting of the horse nail trade, held on Tuesday, at Cradley Heath, it was reported that the majority of the employers had re- fused to acknowledge the notice sent in for an advance of wages. It was contended by the operatives that the present state of trade justified a substantial advance being given, and in order to avert a strike,which would have disastrous effects upon the district, it was resolved to refer the dispute to arbi- tration.

THE STRIBB AT MACCLESFIELD.—The strike of silk weavers at Macclesfield has now entered on the eighth week of its existence, and there seems as little probAbilitS, of a settlement being arrived at as when it first commenced. The operatives express their determination to resist the employer's terms, and, in appealing to the public for support, urge that the question in dispute should be submitted to arbitration. The silk trade is in a most depressed condition at Maccles- field. Large numbers are waking preparations for emi- r gration,__

THE MINERI OP Youtsittug.---A conkTence of delegates representing the miners of Yorkshire met at Rotherham on Monday, and resolved to endeavour to receive at the forth- coming conference at Leeds a general regulation of miners' labour. The proposition is to restrict the men from working more than five days a week, or more than eight hours per day. A desire being expressed that the ccnference should be delayed in order that Durham and South Wales may send delegates, the date was altered to the Bth December.

THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—Although the coal t ale of this district is very quiet as compared with the pre,sure of a month or so back, there has not been the complete col- lapse in the demand which followed the advance in wages and prices this time last year. House fire coals are being taken in moderate quantities ; for the commoner classes there is a fair demand for iron making and steam purposes; engine classes of fuel move off pretty freely, and although supplies of slack are at present tolerably plentiful colliery proprietors generally are asking an advance upon current rates for next year's contracts. Prices are without material change from last week, except perhaps that the slight giving way upon the full advance in house coals is more general. At the pit mouth best facials average from 10s to lOs 61, second qualities from as up to 9s, common round csals for house purposes 7s to 7s el, burgy about ss. aid ordinary slack 3s 6d to 4s per ton. Skipping has been inactive dur- ing the week, owing partly to the scarcity of vessels as the result of the recent unfavourable weather. Steam coal delivered at the high level Liverpool or the Garston docks average 8s to Ss 6d, and seconds house coals 9s to Os 6d per ton.

THE LABOUR lisnuuT.—The labour market shows few important changes, but at some industrial centres there is a slackening in the activity which has prevailed for some time past. On the Clyde shipbuilding remains exceedihgly brisk, but after a long strike the ship joiners have gone in on the employers' terms. A new shipbuilding company on a large scale is contemplated at Newport. The collieries in the principal districts remain generally well employed. In Fife and Clackmannanshire the advance of 15 per cent, in wages asked by the men has been refused. In South Wales the coal, inn, and steel industries are all busy, and in the Forest of Dean the staple trades are all well employed. The textile trades are as a rule fairly busy, but at Leeds manu- factures begin to complain of want of orders. In Glasgow district spinners allege present business to be unprofitable. in the North of Ireland some dearth of weavers is reported. The trades of Birmingham are only fairly' employed, but from Sheffield reports generally are very good. In the Metropolis miscellaneous trades have an average amount of employment, lent some trades at the East End show slacken- ing. In the United States emne important branches of in- dustry are again temporarily depressed. For South Australia assisted passages are again likely to be resumed. The de- mand for domestic servants remains keen both in the colonies and at home.—Laboar News. SIR JOSEPH PEASE ON WAGES IN THE IRON TRADEd.—Sir Joseph Whitwell Pease, M.P., speaking at Middlesborough on Saturday, as arbitrator in the matter of wages claims made by employers and operatives respectively in the North of England iron trade, said he was anxious that the period of award should be as small as possible, because in de,aling with these questions yearly, half-yearly, or quarterly they were not treating them in the broad and wholesome manner that was desired. He looked upon these attempts as merely temporary expedients pending the operation of a new sliding scale. The shorter they made the period of award the better he should be pleased, because it removed the specula- tive element as to what the price of iron was to be; and the more they eliminated the speculative element from wages the better would masters and men be satisfied. The pre- vious scale broke down very much owing to the, period embraced in the ascertainment of prices, and he saw no difficulty in having a monthly or bi-month fee ascertainment, THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—There was a very sluggish market on Tuesday, and with the unsatisfactory reports from Glasgow, buyers were not disposed to operate. The tendency now is to hc,ld back business as much as pos- sible until after the close of the year, and where sellers have to secure orders prices are decidedly easier, but makers as a rule are not pressing for orders, the iron offering in the market at under current rates being mostly through second hands. Lancashire makers of pig iron are firm at 495. to 505., less 2, for forge and foundry qualities, delivered equal to Manchester ; Lincolnshire iron averages about the same figure, and Derbyshire brands about Is. per ton more. Finished iron is rather lower in price, for although makers are still fairly busy they are rolling off old orders faster than new ones are coming in, and good brands of bar iron could now be bought at £0 103, per ton delivered into this district ; some makers, however, still held for 2s. 6d. to ss. per ton more than this. Shipping is quieter, with easier prices. THE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark- Lane Express says :—"During the past week a lower tempera- ture has obtained throughout, and the weather, though fine at intervals, has been rough anct stormy. Some wheat sow- ing has been accomplished, but the arrears of this work cannot have been materially reduced, excepting, perhaps, in Scotland, where the weather has been somewhat more favourable. The markets have been irregularly supplied with native wheat, but farmers' deliveries have been on the whole rather more liberal. For sound and dry samples of good quality prices have been fully maintained in London. Country flour continues to come forward freely, but prices are unchanged. English barley has been hardening in value, but prices generally show no quotable change. There has been a fair demand for new malt at former rates. Oats have been rather against buyers, whilst hems and peas have maintained full values. Trade for wheat off stands in Lon- don has been conducted throughout the week on the level of values current during the previous week. In Liverpool sound wheat has met a fair consumptive trade at former rates, and on Tuesday an occasional advance of id. per cental was obtained for red winter,. Foreign flour has met a dull sale during the week in London. Off coast cargo trade for wheat was virtually at a standstill." ,

IMISCELLANEOUS. The progress of business in the House of Commons will, it is now expected, enable the prorogation to take place on Friday, December 1. The polling at Salisbury on Monday resulted in the de- feat of Mr. Grenfell, the Liberal candidate. Mr. Kennard obtained a majority of 103 votes. Five more bodies were got out of the Dinas Colliery, near Pontypridd, on Monday night. They were buried at the time of the explosion under water. Mr. W. WArthur, M.P., has been created a Knight of the Order of St. Michael and St. George. The same tumour is also given to Mr. Thomas M'llwraith, First Minister for the Colony of Queensland. The Rev. H. Cowgill, who has been nominated to the benefice of St. John's, Miles Platting, of which he was curate under Mr. Green, has decided to accept the benefice, and will shortly present himself for institution. At Yeovil fare on Saturday, a panic occurred in a show, owing to the fear of the people that a performing Zulu was going to assegai them. A number of people were thrown to the ground and trampled upon, and the front of the show was forced out. An interesting civil case, in which Mr. Biggar, M.P., will be defendant, to which reference has already been made In the newspapers, will not come on for trial before February, having been delayed owing to the illness of the lady who is plaintiff. The result of the Leeds School Board election was de- clared on Monday night. There were fifteen seats and nine- teen candidates, of whom eight Liberals, or unsectarians, five Churchmen, Wiii two Roman Catholics were returned, being a Liberal gain of five. The committee of the Liverpool Liberal Association have decided to contest the seat rthich becomes vacant by Lord Sandon's accession to the peerage. It is believed that their candidate will be Mr. S. B. Guion, and that the Conserva- tive candidate will be Mr. A. B. Forwood.

The leading members of the Liberal party in Liverpool recently invited the Premier to a banquet to celebrate the right hon. gentleman's 50th year of Parliamentary service. In reply Mr. Gladstone writes reluctantly declining the honour, "owing to the pressure of Parliamentary duties and the uncertainty as to the date of the prorogation of Parliament."

During a football match at Leeds, on Saturday, between the Dewsbury Club and the Leeds St. Join's, Mr. A. Hat- field, the captain of the former team, was seriously injured by coming in contact with one of the opposing players. He was carried to the infirmary, where it was found that his collar-bone was fractured. The game was stopped after the accident. An unusual amount of gratification and satiafaction was expressed at the Marine Barracks at Chatham, on Saturday, on the receipt of the news that her Majesty had appointed the Duke of Connaught honorary colonel of the Royal Marine Light Infantry. The whole cf the colour-sergeants turned out, and showed in an unmistakable and hearty man- ner their appreciation of this act. THREAT TO MURDEIi MR. GLAXISTONN.—At Bew-street Police Court, on Monday,a man named John Norris Sanders, of 11, Tyndall Buildings, Gray's-inn-road, described as a waiter, was charged with having sent a letter threatening to murder the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone. The letter con- tained the sentence: "All my views are changed as regards your conduct, and I have come to the conclusion that you must die." On being arrested, the prisoner said he wrote the letter in order to bring his case before the public, not to threaten to murder Mr. Gladstone. According to the prisoner's own statement he has been in several lunatic asylums. He was remanded.

His Lordship has been terrified by the conduct of an Administration which includes Lords Hartington, Gran- ville, Spencer, and the Duke of Westminster. He believes that "all the conditions of political life are changed, and that there are now in reality only two parties in the State— Conservatives and Revolutionists." His "political feelings" lean much more to the former than: the latter, and there- fore he sends a modest contribution to the funds of a Con- servative society at Oundle, in Nor tha mp tonshi r e. MONEY "1w CrtancEßY."—A correspondent of the Globe says be public may like to note the remarkable fact that the naw Law Courts have been mainly raised with the sur- plus interest of the suitors' money (see section 6 of Courts of Jostice Building Act. 1365, which gives power to apply £1,600,000 from the " Surplus Interest Fund," for this purpose). "A very good idea of the magnitude of the funds in Chancery," he adds, "may be gleaned from the fact that Gladstone was able to borrow recently for National Mbt purposes no less than £40,000,000 of the suitors' noney ; and, as showing the wonderful increase of busi- ress of the Court of Chancery during the last 100 years, I slay add that in 1780 the funds in Court amounted to about .C 7,500,000 only, the number of accounts being 2,385; whilst in 1880 the funds exceeded £75,000,000, the number of ac- eounts being £35,545. Surely these are cheering figures for the lawyers." DELTM OF TUE EARL OF HARROWBY, K.G.—The Earl of Flarrowby died at Sandon Hall, Staffordshire, on Sunday evening. The deceased nobleman was born on May 19, 1798. He was graduated B.A. at Oxford in 1820, having in :he previous year been elected to the House of Commons as one of the members for Tiverton. He sat for that borough until 1830, and in 1831 was returned for Liverpool, for which he continued to sit until 1847. He was Secretary to the India Board under Earl Grey, and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and subsequently Lord Privy Seal under Palmerston. In 1859 he received the Order of the Garter. Lord Harrowby has always been well known for his ardent pursuit of benevolent objects. A vacancy in the representation of Liverpool is created by the death of this truly venerable nobleman. Lord Sandon succeeds to the title and estates. It is a singular coincidence that the late earl's brother—the Hon. F. Dudley Ryder—should have died on the same day as the earl. He was seventy-six years of age. DELTA OF LORD FITZGERALD.—The Right Hon. Lord Otho Fitzgerald died on Saturday at his seat, Oakley Court, Windsor, in his 56th year. The deceased was the third son of the Duke of Leinster. The death will be deeply lamented ' by a large circle of friends. As late as Tuesday last Lord Otho was in perfect health, and went up to London from his house near Windsor to visit one of the theatres. Returning on Wednesday he complained of neuralgic pains in the face, and considerable inflammation set in. During Thursday and Friday the pain and the inflammation continued, and it was ascertained that blood poisoning had ensued. All the reme- dies that were prescribed were unavailing, and between three and four o'clock on Saturday Lord Otho expired. The rapid progress made by the insidious disease of which he was the victim has, we believe, scarcely any parallel in the history of similar cases. Mn. GLADSTONE ON WORKINGMEN IN PARLIAMENT.— A correspondent recently wrote to the Prime Minister asking whether he did not think more workingmen should occupy seats in Parliament, and whether, in view of the recent pro- posal to introduce Conservative workingmen into the House of Commons, efforts should not be made to secure the return of workingmen to Parliament who bold Liberal views. Mr. Gladstone's secretary replied on the 15th of November as follows :—" Sir,—Mr. Gladstone desires me to acknowledge the receipt of your letter on the subject of the representation of labour in the House of Commons, and I am to say that he earnestly desires to see a large number of workingmen in the House. Representitives of labour should certainly be more numerous in Parliament, and Mr. Gladstone hopes that upon every practicable opportunity workingmen-will be brought forward as candidates for seats in Parliament. He fears that workingmen themselves are greatly to blame that they are not more fully represented in the House of ;Commons." TEE LAND AGITATION IN Sy.—This agitation is assuming a serious aspect. The difficulties of tho authori- ties in maintaining order are increasing, and all attempts to put the law in force have failed. A,t the Braes, the scene of the trouble some months ago, matters are more aggravated than ever. The tenants are defiant, and, in view of the threats that have been used, the authorities find it impossible with safety to serve the writs upon them. The long delay in this service, which is a practical victory to the crofters, has made them more defiant, and now they have the sym- pathy of the Glendale crofters. A county meeting was held at Inverness on Monday to consider the Serious state of affairs in the island. Lord Lovat presided, and the sheriff of the county wrote complaining of the action of the Government in refusing military aid to protect the officers and vindicate the law. It was resolved to send a special police force to Skye, and to permanently increase the county constabulary force by 50 men. A late telegram says : There is a prospect of a settlement being a:Tanged between the Braes crofters in Skye and Lord MacDonald, the latter haying agreed to submit the matters in dispute to arbitra- tion; but it isnot known whether the tenants will accept that arrangement. The attitude of the Glendale crofters is much more serious than, that of the Braes crofters. In Glendale, there are 500 stalwart men, and it is the epininn of the authorities that only a military force can effect the apprehension of some of the number who have committed assaults on the landlord's representatives. TEE MARRIED WOMENS' PROPERTY ACT.—The final meeting of the " Married Woman's Property" Committee was held in London, on Saturday, under the presidency of Mr. Shaw-Lefevre. The proceedings took the form of ft kind of celebration of, the success of the committee's opera- tions in securing the recent Act. The chairman, in the course of his speech, said he believed that a very large number of women in this country were totally unaware of the change that had been effected, or the magnitude of the , operation of the Act which ,lsad been passed. Until the Act was passed married women had no power of contracting, no right of enforcing the law or being sued, and all the personal property that a woman had at marriage became the property of her husband, and all her real property passed into his possession. All that was changed and reversed, and by the Act which had been passed this year, every married woman in the future would have a complete right to hold property of any kind, and of contracting, suing, and being sued. Women who were married would, in the future, obtain the possession of their property without the necessity of endea- vouring to protect themselves by marriage settlements, and they would have a complete right over that property. Wo- men who were already married would, in respect of property which came to them in the future by gift or inheritances obtain possession of that property without the control of theii husbands, and in respect of that property would have a complete right of contracting, suing, and being sued, and, therefore, no greater change had been effected in their life- time.

A deputation representing the British Medical Association waited, on Wednesday, upon Lord Carlingford and Mr. Mundella, to urge the Government to redress by legislation the present deplorable condition of medical education in this country, pointing out the bases on which a remedy could be provided. The ministers expressed themselves in sym- pathy with the views of the deputation. Mrs-rmous POISONING CAsfe.—At New Stapleford, near Nottingham, last Sunday, Mr. Willaece, an engineer at Messrs. Dunn and Co.'s colliery, asked a neighbour for an aperient medicine. A bottle, said to contain magnesia, was handed to him, and the contents were taken both by himself and his wife. Symptoms of poisoning, however, imme- diately set in. With great exertions, the doctors saved Mr. Willance's life ; but the wife, who was recently confined, has now died. The bottle was bought as medicine from a local shopkeeper. SHIPWRECK AND Loss OF THIRTY LIVES.—A telegram from Liverpool states that the iron steamer Winton, 1,900 tons register, homeward bound from the Black Sea with a cargo of grain, foundered on Thursday last near Ushant (French coast), and all on board, except one man, were lost. The survivor was picked up in an exhausted condition by a passing vessel. The Winton was owned in Newcastle-on- Tyne. Her crew numbered about 31 or 32 hands, all told. THE GLASGOW Mont.—At the final meeting of the City of Glasgow Bank, on Tuesday, Mr. Boyd, chairman, con- gratulated the meeting upon the successful termination of all their difficulties. The solvent shareholders had paid £2,750 per £lOO share, whereas if all had met the calls they would have paid only LEX) per share, Mr. John Wil- son chairman of the solvent shareholders, said the latter could look everybody in the face. PROBABLE SETTLEMENT OF THE OPIUM QUESTION.— There is reason to believe, the Pall Mall Gazette says, that a settlement of the opium question may be expected before long. Communications have been actively proceeding be- tween the India and the Colonial Office. All the authorities necessary to settle the dispute are on the spot. The Mar- quis Tseng arrived here recently from Paris. Sir Thomas Wade, the British Ambassador at Pekin' and Sir John Hen- nessy, the Governor of Hongkong, havobeen here for some little time. The exact nature of the settlement arrived at is not yet known; but it is believed that if the Chefoo Con- vention is not ratified, the settlement will be on the lines of that instrument. AN ATTEntPT 'co Mum:am THROUGH JEALOUSY.—An ex- traordinary attempt at murder was made on Friday at Westerhain, Kent. A young man named Sanders, who lived at Harpenden, Herte, some time ago formed the acquaintance of Miss Ellingham, a pupil teacher. Miss Effingham after- wards removed to Westerbam, were six weeks ago she mar- ried Mr. Tippins, a schoolmaster. Some threaten:A:lg letters were received from Sanders by Mr. and Mrs. Tippins, and on Friday night as they were returning home they were met by Sanders, who presented a revolver and fired, the bullet lodging in Mr. Tippin's arm. He fired a second time, but without effect. Tippins then drew a revolver, which he had proeured in consequence of Sanders's threats, and fired. Sim- ultaneously his antagonist fired a third shot, which smashed 'Pippins's watch-ring and swivel, but did not injure him. Sanders escaped, but was arrested in London on Monday nigh,.. It was found that the shot fired at kim by Tippins had entered the shoulder and passed out through his neck. He had a loaded revolver in his possession. Tippins is in a precarious condition. THE CONVEYANCE or- EXPLOSIVES—The public have a right to be protected against the conveyance of explosive materials in passenger trains amongst ordinary parcels and luggage, and without the knowledge of the railway authori- ties and for ance, at all events, public sympathy will be with the railway company in a case heard by Mr. Raffles, the Liverpool stipendiary, on Wednesday. The plaintiffs were the London and North-Western Railway Company, and the defendants the Liverpool Potentite Company (Limited), the charge being that the Potentite Company had sent fifty gun-cotton cartridges and detonators and 51bs. of " potent ite" —a less explosive material than dynamite—as ordinary traffic by a passenger train. The Potentite Company ad- mitted the offence, but pleaded that it was an oversight on the part of their servants. Mr. Riffles, however, very pro- perly regarded the offence as a serious one, and imposed a fine of £lO and costs in each case. Neither railway com- panies nor their passengers should be exposed to the serious danger of having goads of this description unwittingly con- veyed in passenger trains. THE MARQUIS OF QUEENSBERRY AND THE SECULARISTS. —Speaking at the inauguration of a branch of the Secular Union at Stockport, on Sunday, the Marquis of Queensberry said the value of ,organization amongst Secularists must not be under-rated. Catholicism had been able to stand through the efficiency of its organization. Secularism was but the natural outgrowth of the religions of the past. They were mistaken who thought that Secularists cherished a blind animosity to Christianity and its doings. All that Secularists had to say against Christianity was that it had served its time and performed its functions. It had succeeded other re- ligions, and in its turn must make way for its successors. He had himself been excluded from the House of Lords for his opinions. Misrepresentation in his own case bad led to its being said that he wag an Atheist and denied the exist- ence of God. On these grounds alone, and without being allowed to reply, he was actually expelled from the House of Lords; whereas, on the contrary, being an Agnostic, he had never expressed an opinion as to the being of a God, believing the problem too abstruse to be solved by man in his present state. It was not widely known that he was excluded from the House of Lords on account of his secular belief. He should, however, take every opportunity, until he regained his seat in that House, to remind the public of the fact, and to call their attention to the injus- tice done, not only to himself, but to the cause which he represented. MURDER AT GRAVESEND.—The Gravesend police are in- vestigating the circumstances of a fatal assault committed late on Sunday night upon Mr. Thomas Eves, proprietor of the Pavilion Recreation Grounle. Mr. Eves, it appears, according to his usual practice, went to the Pavilion on Sun- day morning, and at six in the evening he spoke to the errand boy, bidding him call at half-past nine and accom- pany him home. When the boy returned he could not get admittance, and, a constable being called, search was made, and Mr. Eves was found bleeding and unconscious in an outhouse at the rear of the premises, whither he bad evi- dently staggered after the attack made on him. His in- juries were found to be of the most serious nature. The eyes and skull were extensively bruised and cut, and at the back of the skull a portion of the scalp as large as the palm of the band had been torn off, apparently by a kick. No clue to the perpetrator of the act has as yet been revealed, but the facts that the outrage occurred upon the grounds belonging to Mr. Eves himself; that he was known never to carry cash or valuables about, with other collateral circum- stances, suggest that the crime is not the act of a robber, but proceeds from motives of personal animosity. Mr. Eves died at the infirmary on Tuesday morning from his injuries. Examination of the grounds show that the struggle between the deceased and his assailant must have taken place just opposite the door of the offices. Shrubs are broken down, and on the opposite side of the path there is a large pool of blood. Deceased appeared to have endeavoured to reach the gateway leading into Wrotham-road, and then to have struggled back alongside the corridor to the place where be was found, there being marks of blood there. A young man who was formerly in Mr. Eves's employ was arrested on Monday night on suspicion. PAINFUL ELOPEMENT NEAR BOLTON.—A painful elope- ment has taken place in the neighbourhood of Farnworth, a township a couple of miles from Bolton, where an elderly ' man, a collier, has been the victim of a base piece of in- justice at the bands of his faithless wife, a comely woman of fifty. Her prepossessing appearance seems to have charmed a shoemaker, and soon an intimacy, which in a very short time ripened into affection, sprang up between the parties. The jilted husband and his spouse had for a long period enjoyed the utmost confidence in each other, and during the whole of their wedded life the man "had never given her a cross word," a fact which, perhaps, few who have entered the matrimonial state can boast. Un- fortunately, such blissful moments, or rather years, could not last for ever, and a change came o'er the scene on the arrival of the son of St. Crispin. The confiding husband remained in ignorance of the conspiracy to rob him of happiness and wife, nor did the lengthened absence of her who had promised to "love, honour, and obey," arouse his suspicions to think that the woman he had taken "for bet- ter for worse," was en route for America. Such, however, was the case, the woman and her shoemaker having set sail together from Glasgow. When the startling truth pre- presented itself to the husband, a search of the house was made only to find that the savings of years (about £80) had disappeared likewise. The feelings of the poor fellow may easily be imagined when he made the discovery, for as he was getting into years it was his intention to retire from his trade of collier and set up in some light business. But his , hopes were doomed to disappointment, and the cobbler, in- stead of sticking to his last, preferred his friend's wife and !gold. Much sympathy has been felt for the victim of this 1 atrocious act.

On December sth, the Duke of Albany will consecrate the Grand Master's Lodge of Mark Masons. On the same diy, his royal highness will receive a wedding gift, presented by the Mark Masons Lodge. The counting of the votes given in the Bolton School Board election was completed at a late hour on Thursday night. The old board was composed was composed of -7 Unsectarian members, 4 Churchmen, and 2 Roman Catholics. To the new board there have been returned 6 Churchmen, 2 Roman Catholics, and 5 Unsectarian members. A melancholy occurrence took place on Thursday, at Wedoesbury. A boy named John Wall had occasion to go to the Patent Shaft and Axle Tree Works, and in return- ing he crossed a temporary bridge over the Birmingham Canal. At the time there was a strong wind blowing, and the youth was blown off the bridge into the water awl drowned.

PROPOSND CONVENE:CCM ON TFIN EGYPTIAN QuEsTiox.— An Exchange Company's telegram from Paris says the 2foreiteur announces in a special telegram that Italy has taken the initiative in proposing a Conference on the Egyptian question, and that Signor Nigrai is about to visit Berlin, Vienna, and London. A man named Wilson, who lost a considerable part of his savings in the late West of England Bank failure, was found drowned in the river between Credition and Exeter, and at the inquest it was stated that of late his monetary loss had caused him to be much depressed. Some feeling is being expressed at the delay in winding-lip the affairs of the bank.

The recent appointment of the Duke of Teck to a colonelcy in the British army is likely to lead to some com- plications, as it does not appear that he has yet been naturalised as a British subject by Parliament, in which case he is believed to be ineligible for the position to which he has been gazetted._ .

On Thursday morning General Sir Evelyn Wood, General Drury-Lowe, General Goodenough, and Admiral Hoskins, who dined with the Queen on Wednesday night, left the Castle for London, most of her Majesty's visitors travelling by the 10-30 Great Western train. The Duke and Duchess of Teck have also left Windsor.

_ The London correspondent of the Freeman's Journal says that Lady Gertrude Douglas, who recently married a young baker attached to the Boys' Home carried on by her brother, the Rev, Lord Archibald Douglas, is not to be turned from the carrying out of her purpose by the sneers or jokes of her fashionable acquaintances. She and her husband have now opened a bakery establishment at Hammersmith. On Wednesday night, a fire broke out on the premises of Mr. Thompson, boot and shoe dealer, Church-street, Mac- clesfield. The flames were first seen issuing through the shutters, and when an entrance Nees effected the interior of the shop was in flames. There was no one on the premises, but the gas had been left alight in the shop. The exertions of the fire brigade confined the flames to Mr. Thompson's shop, whose large stock was destroyed. THE THEFT OF £15,000 WORTH OF BONDS.—Ivan Novitsky was charged at the Marylebone Police Court, on Tuesday, with stealing bonds of the value of £15,000 from Ivan Savitch. The prisoner invited him to his lodgings, and then, after playing chess, assaulted him and made away with the money. He was arrested at Hamburg. The pro- secutor was called as a witness, and described the assault and robbery. The prisoner was then remanded for a week. SUPPOSED MURDER IN LaincssrErt.—On Tuesday morn- ing, a policeman passing down Oxford-street, Leicester, was trailed into a house' where lee found a woman, named Lucy Cement& Patrick, dead at the bottom of the stairs. On ex- amination it was discovered that the neck of the deceased was broken. There were several people living in the house. The husband of the deceased returned home. about midnight under the influence of drink, and it is supposed that a quarrel ensued, and that deceased was thrown violently downstairs. Inquiries are being made. At the Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, Michael Martin, 33, labourer, was indicted for the manslaughter of James Martin, his son, aged 8, at Westminster, on the 13th of October. The deceased had caused his father much trouble by playing truant from the Board School, and on the date mentioaed he again absented himself. On the pri- soner coming home the boy crept under the bed, when the prisoner used a poker to drive him out. The poker struck the boy on the head, inflicting a fatal wound. The prisoner was sentenced te one month's imprisonment. The result of the polling for the Sheffield School Board was declared on Thursday. The Church party returned only five members out of fifteen. The Unsectarians (one of whose candicates, a member of the Society of friends), was at the top of the poll, returned all their candidates, including Mrs. S.R. Wilson. Seven church candidates were defeated; the Wesleyan (Old Connexion) candidate was also rejected; and only one Roman Catholic finds a seat. The new Board shows a decided majority in favour of the energetic and public-spirited policy of its predecessor. Late on Wednesday afternoon, as Police-constable Ellis, of the Kent County Constabulary, was proceeding along a road leading from Cliffe to Rochester, he saw a convict run- ning towards him. Ellis challenged the fugitive to stop. but the man rushed at him, and struck him a violent blow on the head with a pickaxe which he carried, inflicting , serious wounds. The constable, however, closed with his antagonist, and after a severe struggle succeeded in recoil- veying him to prison. Ellis is for the present incapaeitated from duty. Particulars of a,terrible accident which occurred in the Roman Catholic chapel of Mangherow, one of the wildest districts of erounty Sligo, have reached Dublin. On Sun- day morning, while a violent thunderstorm was raging, the congregation were on their knees during mass when a flash of lightning struck the belfry and tore it down through the roof. A dreadful panic ensued, but fortunately only lasted a short time, the priest leaving the altar and calming the worshippers. The heavy stones forming the roof came crashing down into the centre of the congregation and injured many of them. One heavy stone fell on a farmer and broke his back, the injured man dying soon afterwards. The other sufferers are now doing well. 'ln the rush made , to leave the building some injuries were caused. rim PROPOSED MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND AGRICUL- TIIRE.—The Press Association states that, in compliance with a request from the Prime Minister, Mr. Monk, M.P., as presidect of the Associated Chambers of Commerce, has forwarded to Mr. Gladstone a statement of the views of that body in favour of the proposed appointment of a Minister of Commerce and Agriculture. Among the facts and arguments cited in support of the preposed change are mentioned the altered condition of trade and commerce in recent years, the more efficient care and supervision of the interests of trade and manufactures under a minister than when divided among several deparments, greater facility in legislation on such matters as bankruptcy, patents, and partnerships, and dea ing with commercial questions arising with foreign countries, as well as with India and the colonies.

A REMARKABLE TRIAL.—A remarkable trial for perjury was concluded at the Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, before the Recorder of London, and—as a formality, it would seem—before a jury. A man named Richard Gros- smith Goldsmith was prosecuted for parjury by a person named Morris Roberts, formerly of Alanchester and Birming- ham. The two men had had business transactions, and Roberts, upon the evidence of Gelpsmith as to a gold watch which had been left in his (Roberts's) care, was convicted of perjury, and sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment. Upon his release he took means to establish his innocence, and was at last successful. Goldsmith was in his turn prosecuted for perjury, and the jury on Thursday found hi:n guilty. The Recorder, however, paseed by the verdict as a mere for- mality. He announced that he entirely disagreed with it, and passed a sentence which virtually meant the immediate liberation of Goldsmith. The maxim that it is the province of a jury to decide as to the facts of a case is obsolete. The president of the court is now both judge and jury. The polling at Preston took place on Thursday. The greatest interest was taken in the event, and from the hour at which the poll opened the streets were crowded. Mr. Tomlinson had a great number of cabs employed, which plied all day actively. It has been the most warmly con- tested election in Preston for many years, but the proceed- ings were conducted in the most orderly manner. A great number went to the poll from eight in the morning till the breakfast hour, and then again at the dinner hour. Affairs were quiet after that hour until the close of the poll. The boxes were then taken to the Town Hall and counted, and the poll was declared as follows at seven o'clock in tLe evening: Tomlinson 6,351, Hanbury 4,167, majority 2,184. The result was received with great cheering. The majority greatly surprised most people. Mr. Tomlinson, though a Conservative, had the support of the Liberal party. He is a barrister of London, and came forward as a candidate for Preston on two previous occasions. Lord Salisbury was entertained at a banquet by the Scot- tish Conservative Club, ix Edinburgh, on Thursday night. In response to the toast of his health, he crjticieed the Egyptian and Irish policy of the Gevernment. With respect to the former, he held that by the adoption of the policy of their predecessors the Government had attained a temporary popularity, but it would be • the duty of Con- servatives to carefully watch that diplomacy should not be allowed to fritter away what the valour of our soldiers won. In Ireland the results of the Govern- ment's legislation had been to bring about such a state of things that no one who could get his land by bullying would care to take it by buying. Experience told them that agitation would bring about anything. Instead of calling the Liberals a party, he would prefer to call them an alliance, or confederation, whom it was necessary to bribe to keep together; and he felt that the time was coming when the nation would turn from them to the Conservatives, by whom the institutions of liberty, property, and religion had been so marvellously preserved. At the Westminster Police Court, on Wednesday, an application was made to Mr. Partridge, by a person whose name did not transpire, under the following circumstances: —He said that on Monday week he and others attended en a deputation to a member of Parliament at the House of Commons, to express disapproval of the Closure, for which they received one shilling each. On Friday last they attended a deputation to a prominent member of the late Government on the same subject. That gentle- man expressed his approval of the conduct of the working classes in the matter. Applicant was then engaged by two agents to attend a meeting at the West- minster Palace Hotel, on Monday last, to condemn the Government's " gagging " resolutions, and bring men at eighteenpence each, front seat being reserved for working- , men. He brought up eight men, but at the conclusion they were told by the agents, whose addresses they did not know, that there was no money for them. Applicant had paid these men, and sought the advice of the magistrate on the subject Mr. Partridge inquired of the applicant how they got into the house and by whose authority. Applicant could not say. They went into a private room. Mr. Par- tridge could not help him. If be had any remedy it would be in the County Court.
