FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE
THE STATE OF EGYPT.
It is said that the sickness among the British troops in Egypt is now at the rate of 12 per cent. of the total force. Between the 10th and 20Lh nine deaths occurred at Alexandria and thirty at Cairo.

The report of a mutiny among the troops ordered to the Soudan was unfounded, but the prudent soldiers, instead of mutinying, are deserting in large numbers, and they cannot be trusted with arms and ammunition.

It is stated in a Cairo telegram that Sultan Pasha denies that on the 12th July he met Suleiman Daoud when the latter was on his way to the palace, accompanied by four soldiers, for the purpose of murdering the Khedive. Sulei- man Daoud and Mussa el Akhad will be required to sub- atantiate the statements made by them before the Prosecu- tion Committee on 13th inst.

An official denial is given to the announcement made by the Paris Temps to the ef&ct that the British Government bad obtained the Khedive's consent to the cession of the port of Massourah to the King of Abyssinia. The Daily News special correspondent in Cairo says it is amusing to observe that the pretests against the recent ex- posures respecting the treatment of the prisoners grow louder as the treatment improves. If the Zagazig prisoners, the same correspondent adds, had been guilty of gross crimes, there would be more excuse for their being chained and compelled to sleep on the floor, but, as a matter of fact, Shemshi, the greatest culprit, is guilty of nothing more than aiding the rebellion by inflammatory speeches and organis- ing the transport of supplies. Seven other prisoners have been arrested, merely on account of sympathy with the rebels, aud detained in prison without trial, at the caprice of the local Governor.

Preparations for the trial of Arabi and his fellow priso- ners are proceeding rapidly at Cairo. The text of the charges brought against Arabi Pasha, as drafted by Borelli Bey on behalf of the prosecution, have been published. They are four in number, and include abuse of the white flag, ordering the pillage and firing of Alexandria, inciting the Egyptians to arm themselves against the Khedive, and of having " excited " to civil war, and carried devastation, massacre, and pillage ever Egyptian territory. According to the Cairo correspondent of the Times Arabi expresses himself confident of his ability to refute Suleiman's allega- tions, and has furnished his counsel with a detailed account of his movements on the day in question. The Times cor- respondent at Alexandria says he has read the whole of the evidence against Arabi, and is strongly impressed with a conviction of his guilt. The actual presenee of the Pasha at the burning of the city is not proved, but it is stated that the regiments under his immediate command were marched into the city and detailed to the work of incendiarism with as much regularity as if it had been part of their ordinary duty. On the other hand, Mr. Ninet, the friend and coun- sellor of Arabi, has given (in London) testimony which, if it is to be accepted, completely disposes of all the charges against him. Mr. Ninet denies that Arabi ordered or even approved of the looting and incendiarism, and alleges ist the most emphatic manner that the Dictator was the repre- sentative of the whole Egyptian nation.
On Saturday the Auatrieu consul at Naples shot himself dead with a revolver.
The latest news from France is that of a Royalist rising In favour of the Comte de Ckambord.

Ten persons are reported to have been killed by an explo- sion in a powder magazine at Ecuador. It is reported at New York that on the reassembling of Congress, the Commissioner of Inland Revenue will report in favour of a reduction of eight millions of dollars in the inland taxation.

%A. Madrid telegram states that the Rd Book containing the diplomatic correspondence between Spain and England with respect to Egypt and to Gibraltar will be published im- mediately after the opening of the Cortes. A proposal was brought forward on Saturday, in the French Chambers of Deputies, to liberate temporarily the persons now awaiting trial on charges connected with the disturbances at Montceau-les-Mines. A proposition to pro- nounce it urgent was rejected by 384 to 78 votes. A New York telegram announces that the Joliet Iron Mills at Chicago, which employ 20,000 hands, will close on MC. 1. The 'Ruse of this step is the expectation that a reduced tariff and the competition that will ensue will lower the prioe of rails to forty dollars a ton, which is fifty cents under the prices during the extreme depression of 18T7 and 1878. It is said the authorities in Berlin are not disinclined, under certain conditions, to hand over to the English Go- vernmtnt those documents in the lately acquired Hamilton collection of manuscripts referring to the history of Scot- land. The strictest secrecy is still maintained as to the price paid for these antiquarian treasures, but the Ti 17148 Berlin correspondent is assured that one and a half million of marks, or £75,000, is about the sum.

It is reported from the Congo River that the station es- tablished on the Upper Congo by Mr. H. M. Stanley has been attacked by hostile natives. The agent in charge is said to have been wounded. No other particulars have arrived as to the outrage, but the attack is peculiarly in- terestiag at a moment when we hear from Paris of the proposed ratification by the French Government of the treaty said to have been concluded by M. de Brazza. Twenty-seven persons were arrested in Lyons on Sunday on the charge of belonging to an association having for its object the suspension of work and the abolition of the rights of property and nationality. The police effected their arrests at the same hour in different parts of the city, the names of the suspects having been discovered at the lodg- ings of a man apprehended in connection with the outrage at the Theatre Bellecour. Important :papers are in the' hands of the police, showing that the association at Lyons was a branch of the "Internationale."

BOSNIA AND TSUI HBRZEGOYINA..—A Constantinople Cor- respondent says that negotiations have been going on during the last month between the Porte and the Austrian Embassy on the subject of Bosnia and the Herzegovina. A definitive proposal was made by Austria that she should guarantee the Turkish possessions in Europe to the Porte, on condition that all the Sultan's rights over the two provinces should be ceded to her. This proposal was rejected. The belief in Constantinople, the correspondent adds, is that Austria will shortly annex the provinces as the only means of preserv- ing order.

-OPENING or Tan ITALIAN PA.ULIAMSNT.—The new Par- liament of Italy met on Wednesday, and King Humbert, who was received with enthusiasm, delivered an interesting speech. His Majesty congratulated the legislators on the consummation of the political edifice by the operatien of the new franchise. He advised them to devote their labours to social and economic questions, and promised in the name of the Ministry a number of important bills. His Majesty declared that the foreign relations of Italy were in a very satisfactory state, and closed an admirable speech by a glow- ing description of the freedom and unity which had been secured for Italy. Thirty members of the extreme Radical party did not attend the session, because of their refusal to take the oath to the King and the Constitution. Fenn IN A TUAIN.—A fire broke cut in a train while it was travelling on Thursday between Lottringbauseu and Horde Stations, near Dortmound, in Westphalia. The cir- cumstances, which are somewhat mysterious, seem to point to the perpetration of a dangerous practical joke. A pas- senger, who was travelling with several companions in a smoking compartment, had accidentally dropped the lighted stump of his cigar into the slit in the door into which the moveable window-pane is usually let down. Immediately afterwards flames burst forth and set fire to all the wood- work. The smoke and fire progressed se rapidly as to threaten the occupants of the carriage with destruction. Fortunately, however, by their cries and gesticulations they succeeded in attracting the attention of the guard. The train was stopped, and the passengers liberated from their perilous situation before they had received any material injury, the fire being quickly extinguished. It is believed that some person had placed a considerable quantity of highly infl tmmable material between the panels of the car- riage door in a purely wanton spirit of mischief. Ti VISIT OP M. DB Genus TO TUB GERMAN CHIN- CELLOR.—M. de Giers had an audience of the German Imperor on Monday. It is believed at Berlin that the visit of the German En3pe. ror to the Russian Chancellor at Varzin is an incident of "great and happy significance to both Empires." The Feather Lloyd professes to know that the mission of M. de Giers has no reference to any special ques- tion, such as Egypt, but to the general relations of Bussia with Germany and Austria. The Ti MSS correspondent at Berlin says it cannot be doubted that the talk at Varzin re- lated, among other things, to the Egyptian question. "But no one who who knows the past course of German policy in the matter supposes for a moment that M. de Giers was brought to Varzin by anything like the expectation of inducing Prince Bismarck to modify the attitude he has hitherto observed towards England. On the whole the probability seems to be that in going to Varzin M. de Giers was mainly influenced by the general wish to restore at least the diplomatic cordiality which existed between the two Empires before the advent to power of General Ignatleff happened to chill and interrupt it not a little on this side of the Niemen."

div.head: REVIEW OF THE EGYPTIAN TROOPS
div.p: REVIEW OF THE EGYPTIAN TROOPS

BY THE QUEEN. The Royal review of the troops returned from Egypt took place on Saturday, and was a brilliant affair. Her Majesty and Princess Beatrice, attended by the Dowager Duchess of Roxburgh, the Dowager Marchioness of Ely, Major-General Du Plat, and Captain Bigge, left Windsor Castle soon • after ten o'clock, and proceeded to London by special train, arriving at Paddington Station at five minutes before eleven. A detachment of the Horse Guards escorted the Royal party to Buckingham Palace, whence Her Majesty pro- ceeded at a quarter to one in an open carriage, accompanied by the Prince of Wales on horseback, and preceded by an escort of Guards, to the Horse Guards' parade. The Royal carriage was drawn up at the saluting point, and soon afterwards the carriages of the Princess of Wales, Princess Beatrice, and the Duchess of Edinburgh arrived. The review ground presented a brilliant spectacle. A great crowd lined the railings of St. James's Park, facing the Horse Guards, and the route along which the troops marolied was literally packed with spectators. About one o'clock the march past com- menced, Sir Garnet Wolseley leading the staff. As Sir Garnet saluted the Queen, Her Majesty bowed repeatedly to the gallant officer. Following the staff came the naval brigade of 200 bluejackets, who were loudly cheered. The cavalry brigade, which followed, was beaded by Major-Gen. Drury-Lowe. The Royal Artillery next passed, and were the objects of much admiration. The Guards' Brigade, with the Duke of Connaught at their head, next appeared, and were received with great enthusiasm. The Indian contin- gent were next in order, and then came 900 of the Marines,

who met with an enthusiastic welcome. Sir E. Wood headed the Infantry Brigade. The march past closed with the commissariat and transport corps, the ordnance and store corps, the army hospital corps, the army signalling corps, the mounted police, the Post Office Volunteer corps, and the Royal Malta Fencibles Artillery. The whole force was about 8,000 strong. By twenty minutes to two the march past was ever, having lasted nearly three- quarters of an hour. Without delay her Majesty left the ground, followed by most of the members of the Royal family, and returned by way of the Mall to Buckingham Palace. As the Queen returned she met with a most cordial greeting, and after a short stay left the Palace fer Windsor. The troops left the park by Storey's-gate, and Birdcage-walk and Buckingham Palace-road to Grosvenor-gardens, and thence to Hyde Park-corner, Piccadilly, St. James's-street, Pall Mall, and Parliament-street to Storey's-gate, where they were dispersed. At many points along the route the streets were effectively decorated, and immense crowds as- sembled to do honour to the troops. Sir G. Wolseley was cheered all along the line, and the Duke of Connaught received a most enthusiastic greeting, especially in the neighbourhood of St. Jame's-street, Pall Mall, and Trafalgar Square, where the crowd was more densely packed than at any other spot. Notwithstanding the large space of ground here, it seemed to be occupied by one vast and solid mass of human beings, and many thousands of people were unable to go further on until the troops had passed the spot. When the troops arrived at Storey's-gate, no time was lost. The men were immediately dispersed—the Naval Brigade went to the Admiralty, some of the let Life Guards to Regent's Park Barracks, and the Artillery to Hyde Park and St. John's Wood Barracks; the 4th Dragoons later in the day returned to Brighton. And thus concluded a'ceremony which will be long remembered, both by those who took part in and by those who witnessed it. The route of the march was kept by 6,000 naval and military volunteers, and 7,000 policemen. The Right Hon. H. C. Childers, Secretary of State for War, and Mrs. Childers held a reception on Saturday night at the War Office. Among the guests were the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Crown Princess of Germany (Prin- cess Royal of England), the Grand Duke of Hesse, the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh, the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, the Duke of Cambridge, the Princess Mary, Duchess of 'Peck, and the Duke of Teck. The officers of the Indian Contingent were also present. The ceremony of decorating the officers and men of the naval and military forces who had been selected from these having served in the Egyptian campaign for personal deco- ration at the hands of her Majesty was performed at Wind- sor Castle on Tuesday by the Queen, in presence of the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke of Connaught, the Duke of Albany. the Duke of Cambridge, and other members of the It)yal Family. The quadrangle of the castle was selected as the scene of the ceremony, and here an awning was erected with a dais under- neath. The proceedings commenced at half-past twelve. Her Majesty ascended the dais and addressed the troops as follows have summoned you here to-day to confer upon you the well-earned medals commemorative of the short and brilliant although arduoue campaign in which all have done their duty with courageous, undaunted devotion. Tell your comrades that I thank them heartily for the gallant services they have rendered to their Queen and country' • that I am proud of my soldiers and sailors, who have added fresh glory to the victories won by their predecessors. The first to receive a medal at the hands of her Majesty were Admiral Dowell and Admiral Hoskins, and after them came officers and men of the Naval Brigade and Marines, Lord Northbrook attending to point out the officers' names. Sir Garnet Wolseley and Mr. Childers performed the same duty in respect of the army. In pinning the medal on the Duke of Connaught's breast, her Majesty kissed his Royal High- ness. Her Majesty afterwards thanked Colonel M‘Neill for his care of the Duke of Connaught in Egypt.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

HIGHER BROUGHTON V. KNUTSFORD.—PIayed at Knuts- ford. The visitors scored four touchdowns, three dead balls, and one touch in goal, to the borne team one touch in goal. RUNOORN TAM O'SHANTERS 2ND TEAM V. WIDNES ST. MARY'S 2ND TEAM.—This match was played at Widnes. and after a well fought game resulted in a victory for the tiharaters.

WARRINGTON WANDERERS V. WATERLOO VICTORIA.— This match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, and after a well contested game resulted in a draw. Score: Wanderers 1 minor; Victoria 4 minors. RUNCORN UNION V. RUNCORN VICTORIA.—This match was played on Saturday last, on the ground of the former, and after a well contested game resulted in victory for the Victorians by 1 goal, 3 tries, 6 minor points to nil. HIGHER BROUGHTON (A TEAM) T. KNUTSWORD (A TEAM). —These teams met for the first time on the Higher Brough- ton ground, and a well-contested game resulted in a win for the home team, who scored one try (W. Ritchie) and one dead ball to nil. ST. ELPHINS T. OUGHTRINGTOi ROVERS. A match between the above clubs was played on the St. Elphins ground on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the home team by 1 try (Barnes) and 7 minor points to Oughtringt-on 1 minor point. RUNCORN TAM O'SHANTERS V. LATCHFORD TRUE BLUES. —This match was played on the ground of the forraer, and after a tight game resulted in a draw in favour of the home team. Score: Shanters, 1 try and 7 minor points, to 1 try and 4 minor points. WIDNES VICTORIA T. WEST BANK RINGERS. This match was played on Saturday last, and resulted into anothor win by the Victoria.% When half time was called the Ran- gers kicked the ball off, and not long after they secured another point. The score standing when time being called, Rangers seven touchdowns to the Victerias one try.

LANCASHIRE Cur TIE.—WITHNELL V. BLACIIRURNIANS. —The tie in the first round of the Lancashire Cup competi- tion between the Old Blackburnians and Withnell was played over at Withnell on Saturday. At Blackburn the Old Blackburnians were victorious, but the Withnell club entered a protest against the shortness of the ground, and the teams were ordered to meet again. The result was a victory for Withnell by two goals to one. Sr. AWNES RINGERS (WARRINGTON) T. ST. MART'S 1 (WIDNES).—A match was played at Warrington on Satur- day last between these two clubs, when after a remarkably even and exciting game there was a victory for the home team by four tries and one touchdown to nil. The tries being got by R. Knight (one), J. Warburton (one), and E. Nicholls (two). MANCHESTER ATHLETIC T. WIDNES.—These two teams rrTt at Widnes on Saturday, and the home team won by two tries to nil. Teams :—Widnes: J. Briggs, back :3. B. Briggs, Ireland (captain) and Conley, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Burgess, half-backs; Mason, Harrison, Brown, Galli- more, Smith, Williams, Grice, Kenrick and /Eaton, forwards. Athletic: M. Sherlock, back; Bagshaw, Jones and Dearden, three-quarter backs; Timmis (captain) and F. Eaton, half backs; t. Pegg, R. Turner, S. Ashworth, J. Renshaw, H. Reed, C. Shaw. J. Dean, J. Dewse, and H. Crowe, forwards. LATCHFORD (2ND) V. WIDNES RECREATION (IST).—This match was played on the ground of the latter, on Siturday, before a fair number of spectators. It was a most pleasantly contested game, and resulted in a draw, each side having scored a try and a few minor points. For Latchford, Wright, Cannon, Burgess, Renshaw, and Knight played splendidly; and for Widnes, Passey, Hoose, Grundy, and Leather never, perhaps, showed to better advantage; the forwards of both teams played a good all-roand game. NORTHWICH V. RUNCORN (RUGET).—This match Was played on Satarday last on the ground of the latter club. The weather was unfavourable, and the ground very greasy, a state of affairs decidedly in favour of the home players, who bad much the heavier team. North- wich arrived with but thirteen men, but were fortu- nate in obtaining two efficient substitutes in Messrs. Speak- man and C. Pownall. The forward play of both teams was good, whilst the skilful passing of the Ruacorn men was a treat to witness. A very fast game was played during the first half, but after changing ends both sides played much steadier. The rain, which had fallen in a drizzling shower since the commencement of the game, now cleared off; but the wind continued to blow very strongly, and greatly inter- fered with the place kicks at goal. Of the five tries gained by Runcorn, two were secured by Hughes, fr.om one of which the only goal of the match was kicked; and three by Andrews. The try for Northwich was gained by W. Forster. An enjoyable game ended in favour of Runcorn by one goal, four tries, one dead ball, and two touchdowns, to Northwich one try and one dead ball. CHRSHIRR V. STAFFORDSHIRE.—This county match was played at Stoke-on-Trent, on Saturday last, and was wit- nessed by a large number of spectators. Cheshire losing the toss had to face a strong wind. Three minutes from the start Bowcock, with a flying kick 40 yards from goal, scored the first point for his side, the Cheshire goalkeeper misjudging the ball owing to the wind. The Pottery men kept up a continual pressure, but owing to the tine defence were for some time unable to increase their score, Morton stopping some dangerous shots, until Crossland got a fast one past him, and scored a second goal for Staffordshire. Roused by the reverses and by the shouts of the rather one- aided spectators, the Cestrians buckled to their work, and the ball was taken to the Stafford goal, but Maddocks, missed a grand chance, and the ball once more careered down the field. Again getting possession, Plant and Turnbull took the leather the full length of the field, and passing to Bates the last-named promptly scored the first goal for Cheshire. This success was quickly followed by a second goal from the foot of Moore, after anbther fine run on the left wing. At half time the score was two goals each. On changing ends the Cheshire team completely overpowered their Opp- nents. Five minutes from re-starting Plant, from a pass by Moore, shot the ball through, but the point was disallowed on a claim of off side. Immediately afterwards Moore headed a ball through out of a scrimmage, and a few minutes later Maddocks did the needful again. A fifth goal was scored by Bates, Turnbull added a sixth, and after a sharp tussle in front of the Staffordshire posts, Rose scored No. 7 for Cheshire. The game thus ended in a decisive victory for Cheshire by seven goals to two.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 25, 1882.

WE are glad to find that through the vigilance of the Anti-Slavery Society public attention is now being directed to the posi- tion of England in Egypt so; far as it relates to slavery and the slave trade in that country. Last week a public meeting on the question was held in Willis's rooms under the presidency of the Earl of SHAFTESBURY. It was most influentially attended, and the resolutions which were adopted called upon the Government to exert their influence so that the abominable traffic in human flesh may be abolished in the territory under the sway of the KHEDIVE. Since then, several questions have been put to the PRIME MINISTER in the House of Commons with the object of eliciting the views of the Government on this matter, and it is satis- factory to find that everything is being done that can be expected towards the abolition of this obnoxious trade. A few facts bearing on the slave question may, we think, be profitably recalled here. It is now almost half a century ago since the long-maintained and noble struggle against the existence of slavery in British possessions came to a suc- cessful termination. In August, 1833, the Emancipation Bill received the approval of Parliament; and the freedom of slaves in our dependencies was secured by the expenditure of z0,000,c00 of British money. By that Act the complete enfranchisement of negro slaves in our colonies took place in 1838. Ten years later our neighbours on the other side of the English Channel followed our excellent example, and the negroes in the West Indian and other colonial possessions of France were liberated. About the same time, too, the new Republics of South

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 25. 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 25. 1882.

lAmerica declared against slavery. In 1863 the Dutch slaves had their freedom conferred upon them; and in the same year, while the great war between the Northern and Southern States of America was still waging, PRESI- DENT LINCOLN'S memorable proclamation rendered slavery henceforth practically im- possible on any portion of American territory. Two years subsequently a clause was added to the Constitution providing legal security against the re-introduction of slavery into the States. The iniquitous and inhuman trade having thus in almost twenty years received its final death-blow in British, French. American, and Dirtch dependencies and serfdom in the same period having been abolished in Russia —it soon met a similar fate in other parts of the civilised world, and its universal suppression became to be re- garded as only a question of time. In iB7l the Brazilian Government enacted a law which provided for the gradual extinction of the system in that wide empire. Then came the treaty between Great Britain and the SULTAN of Zanzibar which has had the effect of almost extinguishing the nefarious traffic on the east coast of Africa. The Govern- ment of Egypt was almost the last to, profess to take any measures for the suppression of the slave trade, and to profess to stop the horrible traffic in human flesh has been all that the Government of the 'KHEDIVE has attempted to do. As an outcome of Sir SAMUEL BAKER'S expedition to the Nile region, in 1877 a convention was signed between the KHEDIVE and the British Govern- ment which had for its object the total sup- ' pression of the traffic. The sincerity of the KHEDIVE was then doubted in some quarters; but, :at the same time, it was evident that even supposing any efforts were made by him to put down slavery, they would be opposed, if not defeated, by his officers and the army of slaveholders who make it their business to meet the Turkish d&mand for slaves. That the Convention of 1877 has been a dead letter so far is now too well proved; but the Government seem determined ithat it shall not be so in the future. Explorers are apt to overstate facts and are sometimes I given to the use of the long bow; but there is no lack of testimony to corroborate the statement made at Willis's Rooms last week lin connection with the British and Foreign 'Anti-Slavery Society. Mr. FILKIN, a, member of the Royal Geographical Society and a medical missionary, who has made consider- able explorations in the Nile regions, stated Ithat no less than forty thousand slaves crossed annually from the Soudan into Egypt proper for Egypt and Turkey in Asia. The cruelties practised upon these unfortunate creatures were shown to exceed even the cruelties which are to be found recorded in the annals of the Pacific and Western slave trade of the last century; and it was affirmed by Mr. Firocix, that for hundreds of miles explorers are able to trace their way across the otherwise path- less African deserts by the bones of human beings, who, while being conveyed from in- land to the coast, have died from disease or have been wantonly slaughtered by the slave- hunters. We will not dwell on these sicken- ing details, nor enlarge on the extreme inhumanitiwith which these slaves are treated We would, however, have it borne in mind at the present time that this horrible traffic is carried on in a country for whose good government recent events have made us responslle. Whatever may have been our right to interfere in Egyptian affairs, the fact now remains that British arms and British treasure alone have restored order in Egypt. By the bravery of our soldiers and sailors the KHEDIVE is again on his throne, but it is useless to say that he could maintain his authority for a couple of days were he not upheld by English assistance. Now or never, therefore, the Convention of 1877 will have to be enforced. The Government are thoroughly alive to this, and through the PRIME MINISTER on Monday intimated, in reply to a question put by Mr. FORSTER, that they "are very anxious to deal both with the subject of the slave trade and of slavery in Egypt. One of the very first despatches," said Mr. GLAD- STONE, "sent from the Foreign Office to Lord DUFFERIN was upon this subject. There has not been time since his arrival," added the PREMIER, "to receive any report from him-, nor do we know that he has had time to frame a report; but it is a subject which we will by no means neglect, and on which we shall be desirous to pursue a policy in conformity with the spirit of that policy with which the name of this country has been so long identified." The Government have therefore wisely antici- pated the present movement; and we have every confidence their efforts will be pressed to a successful issue. We thoroughly agree with Mr. FORSTER in the opinion ex- pressed by him that were the English Government in the course of next week, to say to the KHEDIVE that they made it a condition of assistance being afforded him that he should at once abolish the legal status of slavery, His HIGHNESS would, after the usual week or two of Oriental delay, assent to our demand. 'I hose countries which followed our initiative of 1833 will now look with interest to our action regarding the Egyptian slave trade, and Englishmen generally will be disappointed if at the close of diplomatic negotiations with Egypt slavery is allowed to be a recognised institution in that country. Many of us regard with little satisfaction the Egyptian expedition. If, however, as one result of our intervention, this hateful system of Oriental slavery be overthrown and finally abolished, that would in itself be some recompense for the loss of life and expendi- ture of treasure which the recent campaign has involved.

was made at the Presseot School Board meeting on ; Monday evening, and it is a proposal which one should think will meet with very general approval among the paterfamilies of Prescot. The charge of fourpenee a week it can easily be imagined will often be found to be a very heavy burden in cases where there are three or four members of a poor family within the age prescribed by the Education Act. It may of course be said that in cases of this kind the parents can obtain relief by representing their poverty to the attendance committee, but this, I as it was very properly pointed out, is the very consequence of maintaining a high rate of school fees which is most to be deprecated. There is a painful sense of degradation felt in laying bare their indigence by the more respectable and sen- sible among poor people which ought not to be in- flicted where it can possibly be avoided. It was argued that the reduction of the fees will mean the increase of the School Board rate, and that it would only be removing the burden from the back of one poor person to that of another. There is perhaps some degree of truth in this argument, but it can easily be understood that any slight increase in the rates will be borne not so much by the poorer working classes as by those who are better endowed with rate- able property, while, on the other hand, heavy school fees are a direct and unmitigated drain on the slender , resources of these who are compelled to send their children to school, when, if they were at liberty, they would much rather employ them, in partially, at least, earning their own livelihood. It is theretore to be hoped that this admirable proposal, when it comes before the next meeting of the Board for the final decision, will meet with a cordial acceptance. The election at Salisbury has resulted, contrary to general exepctatiou, in the return of the Conservative candidate Mr. Kennard, who perhaps is more surprised than anybody else to find he is now ensconced in St. Stephens. How long he will remain there is a Ties- tion on which there may not unnaturally be differ- ences of opinion. It is often the case that those sur- prising and uneipected victories are followed by humiliations. It was the case at Oxford when Mr. Hall was elected, it was the case at Wigan on the occasion of Mr. Powell'.B election, it has been the case in other constituencies which could be named, abd I dare say it will he found to be the case also at Salis- bury. Mr. Kennard has kept the constituency " warm " since hi& ignominious defeat in 1880, and it is said that the "persuaders" which have been used on the present occ ision are of a golden colour. If that should turn out to be true then Mr. Kennard's Parliamentary career will doubtless be short-lived. But whether that be so or not, nobody will be foolish enough to believe that Mr. Kennard's victory is any indication that the people of England are opposed to Mr. Gladstone's procedure resolutions, or as my lord Folkestone elegantly puts it, the "gag; "on the con- trary, the country has long yearned that the House of Commons might deliver itself from the tyranny exercised within its own walls, and it rejoices in th: approaching emancipation. The Salisbury election will long be remembered for one thing, and for one only, and that is the ungentlemanly behaviour to- wards the Premier of that scion of the nobility Viscount Folkestone. True, the noble lord has apolo- gised; but shame on him that tie should have so far forgotten himself. It is idle to speculate on these elections, which:are happily enveloped in uncertainty, but I am disposed to think Mr. Raikes will have very great difficulty in obtaining Mr. Walpole's seat for Cambridge University. Professor Stuart's chances of success increase day by day; and there can be no two opinions which would make the better representative of the two candidates That Mr. R iikes's qualifications are extremely limited is to me, shown by the fact that two gentlemen of his own political persuasion have gone out of their way to condemn his candida- ture, and to appeal for support for Professor Stuart, who is eminently qualified alike by education and position to adorn the seat. The latter is promised the support of the Broad Church, and the High Church party as well; and I verily believe he will receive a large number of votes from the Conserva- tives, who, to say the least, do not take kindly to Mr. R sikes. The Professor has promised, if elected, to relinquish his chair, and to devote all his time to the ' trust which the electors will have placed in him. I am not aware that Mr. Raikes has undertaken, if returned, to cease his connection with the ten com- panies with which he is associated, either as chair- man vice-chairman,- trustee, or director, some of which are to him paying concerns. The electors will, I think, do well to elect Professor Stuart, and save the reputation of the University. "Au Oxford M.P.," writing to the Pall Mall Gazette, says that it would be "almost a degradation if the seat which was once occupied by a Pitt, and a Palmerston, and a Lans- downe should by the deliberate choice of the clerical Tory leaders be awarded to a man of unacademic fame, one who is chiefly known in connection wi;h those City company transactions from which men of higher mind instinctively stand aloof." I deeply sympathise with Mr. Reginald Yorke, one of the members for Gloucestershire. His mind has for some time been exercised with reference to what is sometimes described erroneously as the " Kilmain- ham Treaty," and he has been induced to place on the notice paper of the House of Commons a motion asking for an inquiry into the circumstances attend- ing the release of Messrs. Parnell, Dillon, and O'Kelly from Kilmainham prison. The Prime Minister very generously promised that he woul I not oppcee such a motion if moved by the hon. member to relieve his mind, and Mr. Gladstone also undertook to move the adjournment of the House in order that Mr. Yorke might have an opportunity to air Eimself some even- leg before half-past twelve. But certain members recognise in Mr. Yorke's attitude a downright insult ' to the Prime Minister, while others again think that other business of greater importance should take pre- cedence of the motion in question. Accordingly the other night when Mr. Gladstone moved the adjourn- ment of the House it was successfully opposc d by two of Mr. Yorke's own political friends; but if it bad not been an opposed, Mr. Labouchere had on the paper a series of notices arising out of the Bradlaugh episode which would have taken precedence of Mr. Yorke's notice. Some of Mr. Lebouchere's notices have, how- ever, been ruled slightly out of order, and he has placed on the paper another batch on a variety of sub • jects, such as the Charter of the North Borneo Com pany. Mr. Yorke, I think, had better give up the ghost, for he may rest assured that whatever may happen to his motion there will be no inquiry into the " Kilmainhain Treaty" so-called. The whole thing is a complete farce, and it is a pity M. Yorke should be so foolish as to waste the time of the House on such a matter.

I rather suspect that our neighbour, Sir Richard Cross, is bidding—in the absence of Sir Stafford IsTorthcote—for the leadership of the great Constitu- tional party in the House of 00111t119119. Let your readers, Mr. Editor, take notice how importunate Sir Richard was on Tuesday evening, and again last even • lug, about the Cuban Refugees, and I think they will arrive at the conclusion that tne right hon. baronet means business. Tuesday, observe, was the first opportunity he had. of showing his "go," and he beats the noble Lord Churchhill into fits. Sir Richard will, I confidently predict, be taken down a peg before he finishes. I wonder if he has had any acquaintance with the "Circumlocution offi e." He is a fellah whO wants to "know you know," but he wants to know too much, and he also wants to know it too soon. FLACCUS.

THEFT OF CLOTHING BY WOMEN AT WIDNES . Mary Gillon, an old woman, and Mary Ann Orrell, a married wctnan, were charged with stealing 10 mufflers from Frederick Tebbut'e draper's shop, Anne-street West, on the 6th inst.—Frederick Tebbut, residing in Earlestown, said the kept a shop in Anne-street West, Widnes. The mufflers produced were his property. On Monday morning, the 6th November, he hung them up in a recess at the entrance to his shop, and they were safe there about five o'clock. In another hour he missed them and gave information to the police. The mufflers were worth about 13s.—Mrs. Evason, of 23, Pleasant-street, Widnes, deposed that on Tuesday, the 7th inst., the prisoner brought the scarves (produced) to her house and asked her to purchase them. The prisoner asked 101 each for them, and witness purchased them.—Martha Boscoe, 20, Pleasant-street, said she was a married woman. On the 7th inst. the prisoner Orrell visited her house. She was carrying some scarves which she said she had got from Mrs. Jamieson, who was allowing her something for selling them. Witness purchased some. —Mary Jane Ball, the married daughter of the last witness, also purchased a muffler. Payment for them was after- wards made to Mrs Gillon.—P.S. Strickland stated that on Tuesday he saw a boy in Lugsdale wearing one of the scarves produced, of wLich he took possession. He accom- panied the boy to his home, where he found other two scarves. He atlso received scarves from a number of other persons. Subsequently he went to Oerell's house, where he found the husband wearing a scarf. He took the priso- ners into custody, and charged them with the robbery. Mrs. Orrell replied," My mother got them from Mrs. Jamieson's to make a trifle out of them." Mrs. Gillon replied, "A Scotchman ' gaveithem me for a shilling." Mrs. Gillon now admitted her guilt, but Mrs. Orrell said she knew nothing about the robbery.—Mrs. Gillon was then charged with stealing an overcoat, worth 12s. di., the property of Fredk. Meal, pawnbroker, Anne-street West.—lt appeared that the coat was hung in the doorway of the shop by the assistant, John Dixon, on the 18th instant. On that date, whilst searching the prisoner's house, P.S. Strickland found the overcoat, which was identified by Dixon.—For stealing the overcoat, Mrs. Gillon was sentenced to one day's im- prisonment, and on the first charge she was committed to gaol for a month. Mrs. Orrell was also committed for a month's imprisonment.

A FAITHFUL FOLLONOCR OF BACCHUS.—At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Edward Godfrey, who made his 33rd appearance, was sentenced to a month's hard labour for be- ing drunk at Widnes on the 13th inst.

CHARITY'S REWARD AT 'RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, John Rogerson, a labourer, from Nantwich, was charged, on remand, with stealing a silk handkerchief and 78. 61, belonging to a boatman, named Jacob Baker, and he was corSmitted to Knutsford Sessions for trial. The robbery was committed on the 19th September, when the prosecutor gave the prisoner a night's lodging.

UNCOEN SAVINGS' BANK.—Under the direction of the Commissioners for the reduction of the National debt,returns have been prepared and just made public from the accounts ren.-lered to their office by the several old savings' banks in the United Kingdom. The following relates to the Runcorn bank :—ln this bank there were 709 accounts open, with £22,689 as. 9d. standing to their crelii. During the year there were 1.282 reeeipts from depositors averaging £5 501. 3d., and 743 payments averaging £0 93. 91 The cost of management was £lO5 133. 7d., and the balance with treasurer £491 14s. 9d.

BANKRUPTCY OF A WIDNES SOLTIKTOR.—At the Liver- pool Court of Bankruptcy, yesterday, before Mr, J. F. Collier, judge, Mr. Thomas Beasley, solicitor, appeared to pass his public examination.—Mr. Holland, the trustee, stated that the amended accounts were only just completed. Still, they had been examined by him, aud he was satisfied with them. In addition to that, there had recently been a meetinp,-of his creditors, at which it was resolved to accept a composition of Ss. in the pound, and the resolution would come before the court for confirmation on Friday next.— His Honour said he understood that the proposed cotnposi- tion would come before him for confirmation; and upon that understanding, and upon the accounts being tiled, he should have no objection to the bankrupt passing his public exami- nation. He woald, however, adjourn the public examina- tion until Thursday next, in order that the accounts might be filed; •

AN INCORRIGIBLE VAGRANT AT WIDNES. —Martin May, a young man, was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, on a charge •of vagrancy. • P.C. Barker deposed to discovering the prisoner asleep that morning on Messrs. Hatchinson's chemical works. Supt. Barker said the prisoner had been convict:A on nine occasions for sleeping in chemical works, and sentenced to various terms of imprisenment. In August he was committed for three months. The prisoner said nobody would give him a job, and he could not get lodgings. If their Worships would give him his liberty he would leave the town immediately. Mr. Lewin : You always say that. Mr. Gaskell, junr. (to prisoner): You must go to gaol for three montbs'again.— For a similar offence Lawrence Riley was committed to prison for seven days. FATAL COLLISION ON THE BRIDGEWATER CANAL. - An inquest was held. on , Monday, before- Mr. S. Smelt, the deputy city coroner, on the body of Joseph Hinds, aged 19, waterman, late of 11, Shaw-street, Runcorn. The deceased was engaged on board one of the c mai tug steamers, called the Stretford, which at a few minutes after one o'clock on the afternoon of the 9:h November was going towards Man- cheater. When near Manchester they met another steam tug, called the Heywood, which was on the wrong side of the canal. Each of the tugs had a train of thlee flats, and while trying to pass with safety the .high wind which was blowing at the time blew the Stretford between the Hey- wood and the first of the flats attached. The rope by which they were connec!ed knocked over the smoke stack, and it is supposed that it fell on the deceased and knocked him in- to the coal bunkers. He was taken to the Manchester Royal Infirmary, where he died on Sunday last from the effects. of the injuries he had received. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

THEFT AT CRONTON : REPENTED TOO LATE.—On Wed- nesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., and John Brock, Richard Taylor, a man having the appearance of a labourer, was charged with having, on the 18th inst., stolen a horse cloth, of the value of 19a., the property of Rilph Crosby, farmer, Cuerdley.— It appeared that on-the day in question a tearnsm in named Wrexham was in charge of a horse and cart. He stopped at the Unicorn Inn, Cronton. He went in the public•house, leaving the cloth in the cart. In a short time the prisoner followed him in the house, and then went out again.- When Wrexham went to the cart with the intention of resuinieg his journey he discovered the cloth had been stolen.—Jas. Houghton, the landlord of the inn, directed Wrexham to the police station, and then, whilst in the street, he sew the prisoner creeping along the street to the cart, into which he threw the cloth.—lt was stated the prisoner was not drunk. —The Bench committed the prisoner to gaol for 21 days with hard labour. ' THE SHOCIMTI ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT RUNCORN.— 'At Knutsford Quarter Session, on Tuesday (before Mr. Horatio Llcyd), James Robinson, labourer, forty-nine years of age, was indicted for maliciously wounding his wife Mary, by biting a piece off her lip, under circumstances previously reported. Mr. Burke Wood prosecuted, and Mr. Simpson defended. The jury returned a verdict of " guilty." —Mr. Simpson produced a medil which prisomer hid re- ceived for his services in the Crimea, and also handed in a character from his employers.—The Deputy Chairman observed that it was a sad and melancholy thing to think of a man who had come to the prisoner's time of life, and had served his country with credit, committing such a dastardly and disgusting offence. If it had not been for his previous good character—they heard he had been a steady, inoffen- sive, and quiet workingmen hitherto, and this was probably the result of drink, if the truth were told, and forgetting himself and the manly character he had hitherto maintained —they would have given him a great deal more, for be did not think any punishment would have been too much. Under all the circumstances they would give him as little as they consistently could for such an offence, and that was twelve months' imprisonment, with hard labonr. DONE IT FOR WANT OF GRUB.—A. RUNC FRAUD. —On Thursday, at Runcorn Police Court, Samuel Charles Furness, a man with a wooden leg, was charged, in custody, with having: on the 20;h inst, fraudutentiv obtained is. m fro John Ellis, the landlord of the Foresters; Arms, Canal- Street; and lodgings and food from Win. Jolley by neves of falee pretences.—lt appeared that on the 18th inst., the pri- soner went into the Foresters' Arms and called for a glass of beer and porter. He said he had come form Garston to draw a pension of 3EI from an American Steamboat and Railway Company. On Monday, Ellis again saw the prisoner, who said he had been to the police station to see what time his pension would arrive from London. He stated the superin- tendent had told him that it would arrive about four o'clock. He then asked Ellis to lend him a shilling, and the former did so. Ellis stated he would not have lent the prisoner the shilling but for his statement about the pension.—Mrs. Jolley was sworn, but protested that what she gave the prisoner was given in kindness and not in consequence of the pension he stated he was to receive. —Mr. Superintendent Williamson said he never saw the prisoner until he was locked up on this charge. He had no pension to receive for the prisoner, nor had the latter seen him about one. When charged by Inspector Holliegworth, the prisoner said "I have done it far want of grub; I have been on the spree."—The prisoner said it was very hard that he should have to be committed to the sessions for a paltry shilling, which he could have paid 30 times over if the prosecutor bad waited till this tide.—Mr. Binkes said he had no alternative, and committed him for trial. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WlDNES.—Sermons in behalf of the trust fund were preached in this church on Sunday last by the Rev. J. Billington, of Runcorn. The inclement state of the weather militated against the attend- ance of the congregation, but the collections realised a nice sum. On Monday evening, the annual congregational tea party was held, and there were about 130 persons present. The tables were presided at by Mrs. Wildams, Mrs. ' Betney, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. Scrivens, Mrs. Perry, Mrs. Locke, Mrs. Rutterford, and Miss Cansey. Subsequently a lecture entitled, "Auld lang syne," was delivered by the Rev. J. Billington. There was a good audience, and Mr. Yates occupied the chair. During the evening, the choir sung a number of anthems with much taste; Mr. A. Ogden presid- ing at the harmonium. The lecturer said the word " old" was wonderfully suggestive. It was like a harp from which might come the low sad wail of sorrow or the glad ringing notes of joy. It might mean age with its withered hopes and blighted prospects, the crumbling mansion with the down- fall of ancestral glory and pride ; the decay of national greatness, with its warnings to nations that still survive; or it might mean life ripened, cultured, and purified; friend- ships cemented as with adamant—the solidity and abiding steadfastness of the "everlaring hills." All of them had not the pleasure of looking back upon a peaceful, happy home of childhood, but those who had found the picture indelibly stamped upon the retina ef their hearts. The graphic outline of that old home would never be effaced, not even when its memories were anything but peaceful and happy. The strength of the home was the strength of the nation. Men and women of the noblest stamp ()evilest character were made at home. - If home diacipline and obedience be maintained home virtue and home piety inculcated, thee a nation was strong. Mr. Billin,gton described in eloquent language the various kinds of old folks there were in the world, and the thoughts conjured up by a retrospective view of our "Auld acquaintances." Speaking of the" Old Book," he said some contended the Bible bad had its day: that its glory was departing with the development of science and the advance of reason; that soon its place would be among the misty volumes at the tuck of book shelves, and that then, if man hal any reverence for it, it would be simply " for the sake of auld lang of wearing prophetic garments, but he would pay that never tahVeneLionasndof tnhoetlivbecause e noitsclaiimatuoetnhcee right of while men were subject CO human weaknesses and human sorrows should this old book lose its power over living men, annsodle,hotomebeeaat light dto a rukpnl ei ef te a anndd e nt on oh br t ing to purifytheir haenadrtsco that nothing earthly should overshadow. This old book taught, as no other book did, that there was a common brotherhood of mankind; that high and low, rich and poor, were made of "one flesh and blood," to dwell together; that rank was but an accident of life ;. that outward circum- stances were not the data for heaven's judgment, but inward dispositions and motives; that man was above the rank and station in which he mieht be placed. As Burns said, " The rank is but the guinea's stamp ; the man's the gowd for a' that." Our duty was to work and pray that this universal brotherhood might be recognised, and that men everywhere might be bought to see that their own weal was bound up in that of their felloAre.—The proceedings ceucluded with the usual votes of thanks.

tions for the vacancy on the Board of Guardians are as fol- low :—Mr. John Matthews, Jenthermerchant, Victoria-road, nominated by Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junr., Woodend Chemical Works, and Dr. O'lieeffe, Barnton House ; Mr. Samuel Saddler, provision merchant, Lugsdale Villa, Lugs- dale-road, nominated by Mr. Richard Farrant, Appleton Villa,Albert-road,and Mr. Joshua lifidwood,Bank Villa, Hels- by, Cheshire. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.—For the purpose of further considering the new bye-laws of the Highway and Health Committee, a Special meeting of Widnes Local Board was held on Thtirsday.' Mr. Kershaw occupied the chair, and there were Also present Dr. Booth, Messrs. E. Carey, T. Handley, D." Wright, Midwood, David Foster, Webster, I Sadler, Allen (clerk), Higginson. (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspector).—Mr. Kershaw animadverted very Strongly upon the uselessness of the model bye-laws issued by the Local Government Board, and remarked that it was almost a waste of time for the Local Board to bother with 'them. He was quite certain that in a few years they would be Superseded by others, and the Board would have again to consider the subject. What they were now doing was simply a waste of money. The old bye-laws were sufficiently stringent for Widnes, With the exe6ption of a few clauses with ' regard to the Realth Department. Mr.. Carey pointed out that the old bye-laws, if they adhered to them, would require printing, whilst the new bye-laris were in type. The old bye-laws for the Rath Committee were very inadequate, and he cotild not consent to the labours of years being ren-. dere(' useless in the way suggested by Mr. Kershaw—hv rejecting the new bye-laws, Nyhich had been passed over 12 months ago. The only thing to be decided now was whether they should print them.—After a little further discussion, 'during which it was etited that the apense of printing would be from £lO to £l5, it was decided that the new bye- laws should be printed.—This was all the business. A WIDNES WOITNDING CA.511. t the Liverpool Assizes, on Thursday, a young man named John Riley was !Charged with wounding Win. Radcliffe, at Widnes, on'the 11th inst., with intent to do him grievous bodily harm—Mr. Lumb prosecuted, and Mr. Segar defended.—Both young men reside at Widnes, and on the night in question they attended a dancing class which was being held, at the Mersey Hotel. Neither spoke to the other at the class, and about half:past ten o'clock the prosecutor and some other young men left the place. They walked along Waterloo- road, and when at the corner of-Pitt-street the prisoner, who was accompanied by a young woman, passed them. When the prisoner and his companion had got about 60 yardS in front of the prosecutor and his friends, the prisoner left the young woman and came back to the prosecutor and asked him in an offensive manner if he "had been making a fool of him." The prosecutor denied having done anything of the kind, and, without saying more,' the prisoner took hold of the prosecutor by the shoulder with wire hand, and with the other struck him a sharp blow on .the left breast, after which he walked away. The prosecu- tor noticed nothing at the time, but after walking about a hundred yards he saw that he was bleeding. He at once went to a surgery, where it was found he had a slight punc- tured wound on the left breast, near the heart, such as -might have been caused by a knife, or some other sharp in- strument. The prosecutor, in his evidence, stated that he did not see any knife in the prisoner's hand. When charged before the magistrates the prisoner denied having struck the prosecutor at all. A verdict of guilty was returned, and the prisoner, who had been previously convicted, was sentenced to five years' penal servitude.

PROPOiED REMOVAL OP A LEVEL CEOSSING AT, WIDNES. —The London and North-Western R dlway have given I notice that they intend to apply to Parliament next session 1 for powers te abolish the Anne-street level crossing, and to substitute in its stead a new street with a bridge over the St. Helens railway. The application asks for power "To make a new street commencing by a junction with Anne-street East, in Widnes, 60 yards or thereabouts, east of the Anne- street level crossing on the company's St. Helens railway, and terminating by a junction with Lugsdaletroad, 60 yards or thereabbuts north-east of the junction therewith of Anne- street West. And to stop up, and discentin ue, and appropriate to the purposes of their undertaking the /site of the saidlevel crossifeg, and so much of Anne-street aforegeid 39 is situate , between the said level crossing and the commencement of the said intended new street, and to remove the existing footbridge at the said level crossing." It is much questioned whether this will not have the effect of removing one incon- venience and substituting one al.nost as great. The dangers 1 of the level crossing will of course be at an end, but the new road will cause such a diversion of traffic, which will have to travel a very devious road that it will find very little favour from the public. The route now proposed to be taken is as follows:—It will commence by a junction in Anne-street East at a point some 60 yards east of the present levelnrossing. Thence it will proceed northwards through Messrs. Evan's yards and the boiler works of Mr. David Foster, and along Penn-street and Pearson-streeL Turning west. it will now proceed to the north side of Edtnund-street, and crossing Victoria-road at the Ship Inn, tertninates in Lugedale-road opposite the end of Oxford-street. If this route is adhered to, the new road will be about 300 yards long. The railway, as we have intimated, will be crossed by a bridge at an inclination of one in thirty. One of the disadventeges of the new way wiii be that Messrs. Muspratt's chemical works, the works of the Widnes Alkali Company, and the other manufactoties which are situated immedietely beyond the crossing will be much more difficult of access than they at present are. I But the Local Beard, weeundersteni, are preparing, or have 1 prepared, an alternative scheme which will probably be ' Bubmitted to the next meeting of members; and the devious route we have described may not, After all, be adopted. The Waterloo-road crossing, which causes the most inconveni- ence,and which the Local Board are continually endeavour- ing to get removed, is not mentioned in the application. A GRIEVED THIEF AT RI7NCORN.—Before Mr. William Benkes, at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, George Radford was brought up on remand charged with stealing, on the 31st July, 1880, a coat, the property of Edward Imison, pawnbroker, Church-street, Runcorn.—From the evidence of Mr. Imison, Mr. Wm. Gorman, detective ser- geant, Wigan, and inspector Dutton (formerly of Runcorn), it seemed that in August, 1890, the prisoner was appre- hended at Wigan for some offence, when it was discovered that he was wearing the stolen coat, which was identified by Mr. Imison. 'rue prisoner was apprehended by Inspec- tor Hollingvrorth on the 15th inst.—The .prisoner stated that two years ago he had suffered for the offence with which he was charged in connection with several other offences, when he was brought into the police static°, ho had no idea that he should be charged with this old offence, and when he was "thrust in that hole below," he felt that he would rather be anything than a human being. If he could have sunk through the floor and the town hall upon him, or have crept into some small hole, hidden from the gaze of the world, he would have done so. —Mr. Johnson said the m igietrete WIS not concerned with the prisoner's feelings, but whether there was any evidence upon which to charge hire at the sessions.—Tbe prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Kuutsford session,.-Ir.l Superintendent Williamson said there was a second charge against the prisoner of stealing six pairs of stockings, the property of Samuel Williams. He purposed withdrawing the charge as he did not wish to pile the agony on the poor man unnecessarily.—The prisoner was then charged with having, on Saturday, the 11th November, feloniously stolen a guernsey, the property of Samuel Williams.—Mr. Joseph Beesley, the manager for Mr. Williams, said the guernsey was hung at the shop door about eight o'clock on the night in question. About eleven o'clock the same night, he missed it.—lnspector lolling- worth said he apptehended the prisoner in Bridge-street, on Vv'ednestley, the 15th inst. lie was then wearing the guernsey produced. He afterwards charged him with steal- ing it, and with receiving it knowing it to have been stolen. He replied, "I will take my dying oath that not a thing have I taken since I came to Runcorn. If a man has had a bad name he may as well be hanged. That guernsey cam from Paddy's market, and I paid 95. 6(1. for it."—Prisoner now said that in future, if he only purchased an article of the value of is., he would have a bill made out to show for he came by it.—Mr. Bankes committed the prisonerhow , trial.

div.head: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.

I see the advertisement of the Manchester Ship Canal Scheme is published, and a perusal of it shows how ambitious the "scheme" is. Parliamentary powers seem to be sought for dealing with or absorb- ing: the rights of every township abutting on either bank of the Mersey from Garston to Manchester. So far as Runcorn is concerned very extensive powers are sought, as possibly the Old Quay Canal and Docks may become an important base or centre of operations, and the Board of Commissioners should at once place themselves in a position to see that the interests of the town are not interfered with in any arbitrary manner. It should not be forgotten that Runcorn is a free port, a position only attained after many years of waiting and agitation; and to sanitary requirements the Commissioners should be fully alive and not allow the sewer out- lets to be cut off or interfered with to the disadvantage of either present or future require- ments. The difficulties now experienced in sewering Higher Runcorn, consequent on the apathetic or quiescent attitude of the Authorities, during the pass- ing of the London and North-Western Railway Act for making the bridge over the Mersey, and the inevitable expense of coping with those difficulties should be a sufficient incentive to prevent any future error of a similar nature. It seems strange the Corti- missioners have no Parliamentary Committee, as such a committee woull naturally take cognisance of questions as they arise; but steps should be taken before the next session of Parliament to conserve the interests of Runcorn either by friendly opposition or arrangement. -

UNLAWFUL lIA.WILiNG- AT RuNaatax.—At RULICOrII Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. John Bruudrit, Richard Tilley was charged with acting as a podlar, on the 18th instant, without having a certificate. —The prisoner, it appeared, was in possession of a cancelled certificate, wh;ch he said he thought he was at liberty to use.—Mr.Supt. Williamson said the prisoner was cautioned on the previous Saturday not to offer anything for sale without renewing the license.—The prisoner had been con- victed of a similar offence in June, and the Bench sent him to gaol for a month. SAIS lIAGIIZ'S MINSTRELS AT RUNCORN' PUBLIC HALL.— Our readers will notice by reference to the advertisement column that this celebrated troupe are advertised to appear on Monday and Tuesday next, as above. It is but lately they have returned from the United States, where they met with unprecedented success, the entire Puss being unani- mous in their praise. It is certainly saying ,a great deal for Mr. Hague's confidence in the excellency of his company taking a troupe of niinstrels to the home of its birth, and when the criticism was sure to be hypercritical. That his success was merited we feel sure, and we strongly recom- mend all who enjoy good music, combined with a hearty laugh, not to juiss this opportunity of witnessing this first- class combinatioß .of talent.

THEFT OF A LAMP AT Rtexconer.—Elwara Filkin, a young man, was charged at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, with stealing a 'amp of the value of 155., the property of Philip Speakman. The prisoner was captain of a boat be- longing to the prosecutor, the canal boat "Heaton;' which, on the 12th November, was lying in the Bridgewater Canal, near the "Green Inn." The temp wet safe in th 3 cupboard on that day, but on the following Thursday it was missed. The boat of which the prisoner was in charge was joined to the " Heaton" on the 12th inst. On Sunday morning Inspector Hollingworth went to the prisoners house in Stone-street, and in a cupboard he found the lamp produced. The prisoner was informed he would have to go to the police-station, when he stated he gave 3s. 6d. foe the lamp to a man on the road. When formally charged the prisoner said "I didn't steal it. I never stole anything be- fore." The prisoner now pleaded guilty, and he was sen- • tenced to 21 days' imprisonment with hard labour. THEATRE .ROYAL, RUNCORN.—After being closed a con- siderable time, this place of amusement was re-opened on Saturday evening, when it was crowded. The tragic el piece "Gun Gath " was effectually put upon the stage, while the acting was of more than average merit. Mr. Ottley is to be congratulated upon the change which has been inaugurated in Runcorn. Viewed from the outside the theatre has a far from prepossessing appearance, but inside it is bright look- ing, comfortable, and lacks that suffocating closeness which characterises some theatres. Few, if any, towns of the size of Runcorn, possess a theatre of the same dimensions, and fitted up with the same excellent appointments. The scenery is new and well chosen, and added much to the effective representation of " Glin Gath." We wish Mr. Ottley all succes3 in endeavouring to cater for the middle classes, who will find in the theatre nothing to which they can object. To-night (Saturday) the dramas "Jessie Vere " and "Robert Maceire " will be put upon the boards. Next week "Shamus O'Neil" will be performed, but on Friday will give way for "East Lynne." SUDDEN DEATH AT THE WORKHOUSE, DUTTON.-011 Wednesday, Mr. Thomas Bettley, formerly well known in Runcorn as a fishmonger, died, under very painful circum- stances, at the Union Workhouse Dutton. About two o'clock on the day named, the deceased applied to Mr. Wright, relieving officer, tor an order of admission to the workhouse. He did not receive the order, but about five o'clock he was admitted to the workhouse. It was supposed that he had walked from Runcorn, as he appeared to be in a very feeble - state. He was so weak and ill that he was put in the hospital. In the evening, as the nurse was going through the wards, she observed that Bettley had grown seriously ill, and she told Mr. Janes, the workhouse master. Before Dr. Mounts arrived, at about twelve o'clock, Bettley had ex- pired. The doctor's opinion was that the deceased had suf- fered from disease of the heart. The circumstances mere reported to Mr. Ridgway, the coroner, who did not think it necessary to hold an inquest. Years ago Bettley was a well- to-do fishmonger in Runccre, but owing to the unfortunate drinking habits of the deceased the business was neglected and fell to ruin, so that he became utterly penniless, and dependent upon the charity of those around him. THE WIDNES Doess.—The London and North-Western Railway Company have given notice of their intention to apply to the next Session of Parliament for the following powers in regard to their docks at Widnes and Garston : "To empower the Company at and with respect to their Garaton Docks and their Widnes Docks respective'y, to set apart and appropriate to the use of any steam and other Vessels and of any Canal Rtilway or other Company and of any person or be.dy of persons and for the purposes of any particular trade any portion cr portions of such Docks or Dock and of the berths, wharves, quays, yards, warehouses, jand other works and conveniences at or connected therewith respectively and to make recover, and enforce such charges. rules and regulations in respect thereof as mey be prescribed or provided for by the iniended Act. To empower the Company to grant and issue certificates of the warehousing or storing of goods at their Ciarston Docks and their Widnes Docks respectively and to grant and issue warrants for the delivery of goods so warehoused or stored and to make pro- vision with respect to the transfer and delivery of such ! goods and with respect to the tenor and effect of. such cer- tificates and warrants, and otherwise in relation thereto." A VIOLENT PRISONER AT RtiNTORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Win. Bankes and Mr. John Brundrit, a sailor named Jack Robertson was charged with being drunk and disorderly, in Fryer-street, on the pre- vious evening, and also with having, at the same time and place, assaulted P.C. Morris whilst in the execution of his duty. The prisoner pleaded guilty to the former charge, but stid he remembered nothing about the latter. It ap- peered that about a quarter past eight, on the previous night, the prisoner was ejected from the Blue Bell Inn, and th 12 commenced to create a disturbance in the street. The con- stable requested him to go away. The prisoner immediately ' seized Morris by the throat, savagely kicked him, and knocked him to the ground. With the assistance or a num- ber of people the prisoner was secured, and whilst being conveyed to the police station, he acted in a most violent manner, kicking right and left. He bit the cheek of the constable in a somewhat serious manner. Mr. Superin- tendent Williamson said the prisoner was an entire stranoer to the town There was a witness present, named Wright, who rendered very greet assistance to the police. The prisoner was the most violent man he (the Seperintendent) ever saw in his life.—Dr. McDougall said the constable went to his surgery about "nine o'clock. He was covered with blood, and he was very much scratched in various parts of the body. Under the chin WAS a wound which might have been clusel.by a bite. His knee and right leg were much scratched and torn, as was also his left hand. He was so much exhausted that he (witness) felt it his duty to re- commend the Saperintendent to send him home for the night.—Mr. Bankes said there was no doubt the prisoner was a violent, brutal fellow, and it was quite time that he should understand that he could not do what he liked. The police must be protected in the execution of their duty.—On the first charge, the prisoner was tined 103. and caste, or in de- fault 14 days' hard labour; on the second, he was fined .fes and costs, with the alternative of two months' imprison- ment. HOW TO CURE THE CR& VING POR STRONG
DRINK.

Sir,----The following prescription, which any druggist will make up, has been found very helpful, by God's bless- ing, to those who have been drunkards and who find it hard to- conquer the craving for stimulants. You will confer a boon by placing it within the reach of any who need it, and are not already acquq.inted with it :—Sulphate of iron, five grains; magnesia, ten grains; peppermint water, eleven drachms; and spirit of nutmeg, one drachm.— 'Yours, kc., R. J. WARD. St. Helens, Nov., 1882.

THE WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY AND THE LATTER DAY SAINTS. Sir,—From a placard appearing upon the walls of our town I notice that one of these apoz=ties of latter-day saintli- ness and morality—doubtless a "much married" man—is to deliver a lecture in the Co-operative Hall, on Sunday next. I understand that the Warrington Co-operative Society has two objects at least, one being to assist its members to save money by enabling them to buy cheaply, and the other to improve their social, intellectual, and consequently moral faculties. Some time ago the local admirers of Mr. Charles Bradlaugh endeavoured to obtain the use of the Co-opera- tive Hall for the purpose of hearing him deliver a lecture— net necessarily of an anti-theological character—but because of the well-known Atheism of the gentleman in question, the religious (?) bigotry of the majority of the members prevailed, and the permission sought was refused. Those who know Charles Bradlaugh, even by repute, know him to be a man against whose morality (as we understand the word) his bitterest enemies are not able to say a single truthful word. With his Atheism I have not the remotest

sympathy, but I must say that when the Co-operative Hall is permitted to be used for the purpose of propagating the principles of a sect whose doctrines are not only opposed to the civil laws of our own country, but are in direct opposition to the apostolic injunction that a Christian should be the husband of "one wife," and at the same time are an out- rate upon morality and decency, I am somewhat at a loss to undeistand the consistency of the action of the society in 'the two cases. It looks to me like "straining at a gnat and •-swallowing a very nasty camel."—Yours, LEX. Warrington, November, 1882.

div.head: REV. E. C. E. CARLETON AND PATRONAGE IN THE CHURCH.
div.p: REV. E. C. E. CARLETON AND PATRONAGE IN THE CHURCH.

Sir,—lt is a most curious fact that this individual takes every possible opportunity of sneering at dissent; in his speech at the Diocesan Conference the other day, with his characteristic Christian charity?) and regard for the truth(?) he made use of statements the facts for which exist a great deal more in his own imagination than anywhere else. Sup- posings the case to which he referred to be at all numerous (which everybody, incluiting Mr. Carleton knows is not the fact), viz., that dissenting ministers are subjected to the tyrannous dicta ion of the rich men of their congregations, it would not, in the slightest degree, justify the present abominable character of the sale of Church livings, by which the spiritual mission of the Church has become, in many cases, obsolete, and that of the " huckster " substi- tuted. But there are other evils in connection with church patronage as at present constituted which Mr. Carleton wisely ignored, and one of them I will refer to. Sometimes a rector or vicar, owing to his multi- farious duties, or some other cause, is com- pelled to employ a curate to assist him, and it not infrequently happens that the curate is the better man of the two, and the most popular with the parishioners. Then follows jealousy on the part of the master towards the servant, and the latter receives his summary dismissal. He has no one to whom he can appeal with any hope of suc- cess, and is left to fight his battles as best he can. We have had lots of these cases in Warrington within the last 20 years, and for anything I know, possibly within a very recent period. The petty persecutbn to which these poor curates are subjected by their masters (?) is at times dis- gusting. I have heard of a case where the head parson's wife, acting no doubt witis her husband's sanction, frequently attended the mission church where the popular and eloquent curate preached, that during the whole of the serenon this lady could be observed reading a book. It is satisfactory, however, to know that the days of church patronage and tyranny of every kind are numbered, and with the end of them will come an incalculable blessing.—Yours, Warrington, Nov., 1882.
