MORRIS.

A presentation of a most gratifying character. vas made to Mr. Thomas Morris, manager of the Pearson. told Knowi„ Coal and Iron Company's ironworks, Warri,,ten, an Satur- day evening, in the Assembly Room, at Lion Hotel, by the workmen in the employ of the U,. eftre t.....5e m proceedings were prefaced by a knife and fork t,.4., workmen with their wives sat dowrAt t which about spa o and afterwards the chair was taken by Mr. S. Beaman, ar there were also present Mr. and Mrs. Morris, the ex-'1,413„0,. at (Alderman Pickmere), Mrs. Pickmere, Rev. S. and Mr. Robinson, Mr. C. M. ' , Mrs. Wilkinson, Miss Weldon, A-Ivy (Wigan), Mrs. S. Beaman, Mr. tupd Mrs. R. Rudge, Mr. and Mrs. Mrs.andMr. sT. Griffith, mPri.lki.n•tp,.., ac. 4 Mrs. Fieldlaotose, Mr. and Mrs. Sheargold, (Wigar7., and. -sewral employes from the ironworks of the ~ Pearson and Knowles Iron Co., Limited, Wigan; Messrs_ Critchley, MiKington, rerry, Milner, Davies, Hwhaliclfhorhda,dDiojet,„ „en— C. Price, and Isaac Biddle. The presents, supplied by Messrs. Lloyd, Payne, and Amiel, wi'Alesale jewellers, Manchester, consisted of a very fine real bronze clock an&vases, relieved in front and sides with e,srceptionally fine band-painted porcelain. The clock strikes the hour and half hour upon •a beautifully toned gosig. The clock and vases had been pronounced by an ex- perienced and independent authority to be very unique in design, and the timepiece one of the finest productions of the clockmaker's art. They were exhibited on a table at the upper end of the room, together with an illuminated address of exquisite design, executed by Mr. T. Pilkington, who is employed by the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. The address, which is designed after the style of the 15th century, and is enclosed in a handsome 'gilt frame, read as fellows:—" We, the employes of the forges and mills de- partments of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Com- pany, Warrington and Wigan, present you with this address aad other tokens of our esteem, in acknowledgment of your valuable services and constant attention to our varied in- terests, more especially your untiring efforts in establishing a Provident and Accident Society, by which we have been brought into closer sympathy with each other. We also ad- mire your high personalqualities, by which you have attained to yoar present honourable position, and hope you may long be spared to us. Wishing you prosperity in this life and happiness in that which is to come." The CITAIRMAN said, as they were no doubt all well aware, they were met together that evening to present to their esteemed friend, Mr. Morris, the beautiful presents which they saw before them. It was usual to do this sort 1 of thing at some important epoch of one's history. For instance, on the attainment of one's majority, or perhaps on the occasion of a marriage, or the birth of a son and heir, and very often when a person was resigning office or tear! ing his situation. But under none of these circemstancee were they making the presentation that evening, nor were •they making it for any selfish purpose or sinister motive. (Applause.) It was the outcome of their continual con- fidence in, and the spontaneous:expression of their good will towards, their friend Mr. Morris, in acknowledge- ment of his valuable services and constant attention to their varied interests; and also in appreciation of the high personal qualities by which he had attained his present honourable position. It was by no fluke, by no lucky turn in fortune's wheel, that Mr. Morris had gained the honourable position which he now held, but it was by his indomitable perseverance in trying to attain to some-' thing noble; and when they considered his early disadvan- tages, and the tremendous difficulties under which he laboured, their appreciation of him was enlarged andtheir admiration of him increased. (Applause.) It was by gleaning knowledge here and information there, by constant application to this subject and that, by gaining mastery over this science and that, that he had been pre- paring his way, and qualifying himself for, the position which he now occupied. (Applause.) And now that he bad made for himself a name, he was not inflated or carried Sway by pride, but he was characterised by strong common sense, sound judgment, and a thorough knowledge of every- thing that pertained to his office. His exceptionally deep isnowledge of the iron trade constituted him one of the highest authorities in the country on that subject. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Morris's downright honesty of character and purpose, and straightforward expression of the true con- victions of his mind were too well known to need any com- ment from him. He was sure that there was not one present who did not feel proud to hold a situation under such a man and such a manager. (Hear, hear, and ap- . please.) The toast of " The Queen " was then proposed by the CHAIRMAN, and it was drunk with musical honours. "The Prince of Wales, and members of the Royal Family" was next proposed and honoured, after whish Sir. C. Price gave a song, for which he received an encore. Alderman PIC/MERE proposed the "Town and trade of Warrington." He said the town of Warrington was not _what it was 30 or even 20 years ago, and the progress it had made was owing in no small degree to their Staffordshire friends. He could well remember the time, 30 years ago, when there were no iron works in Warrington, and he could remember seeing the first furnace he saw in his life, and that was in Dallam-lane. At the time there were no houses about the works, but now the works was one of the largest in the kingdom, and surrounded by houses in every direction. He could also remember Warrington when it was what might be termed a large village-when the principal trades were pin. making, tanning, glass-making, file-making, with one cotton mill, and that was at Latchford. He thought when he had mentioned these he had mentioned all the works that existed in Warrington 50 years ago. At that time butter was sold in Buttermarket-street, and in that street there is a pillar beyond which no butter had to be sold. Pig Hill was where it is now—(laughter and applause)—and he had no doubt if their famous Town Council would only let the poor pigs alone it would remain there a considerable time longer. (Laughter and applause.) They would all know the Bride- well. (Laughter.) Well, that now covered the site of what used to be called in Warrington the "Yarns Trough," and at that place was the Running Pump, se called from the fact that tbere was a stream of water continually running from it, and here the people used to bleach the yarns. He was mentioning these simply to show how the town had altered within his recollection. He had heard people say that the town and trade of Warrington seemed to flourish what ever occurred in ether towns, and he thought if they could always boast of such men as Mr. Morris the town and trade would go on and prosper as it had done in the past. (Hear, bear, and applause.) He thought that they would all thank the Staffordshire men for coming forward and doing what they had done for Warrington. (Hear, hear, and applause.) If the friendly feeling which was at present shown between masters and men continued, the town and trade of Warrington would always prosper. (Applause.) Mr. Tnoasas PILRINGTON, in responding, said he con- curred in what the ex-Mayor had said, and he thought if they got all the things that had been promised them, such as the Ship Canal, Warrington would be even more pros- perous than it had hitherto been. (Applause.) Three hearty cheers were given for the ex-Mayor, and I Afterwards the audience sang "He is a jolly good fellow." 1 Alderman PICKMERR said that was not on the progrnmme, 1 but he thanked them for their kind expression of good feel- ing towards him. l The toast of "The firm " was then proposed by Ur. BUNCH, who said that no company deserved to succeed more than the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. During the six or seven years of depression in the iron trade the 1 workmen of that firm had suffered less than those of any I other in the trade, and this showed that they had gentlemen as their employers who were able to carry the concern through both rough and smooth, and he was sure .they would all wish with him that the time would be far distant when there would be any break in their ranks. He had been about eight years under Mr. Morris's I superintendence, and he had always found that gentle- man willing to listen to any reasonable complaint that Ihe had occasion to make, and if he could remove the grievance he had alway% found him willing to do so. Mr. Mounts briefly responded, and said that the success of the firm was due to the discretion of the masters, coupled with the ingenuity of the workmen. (Applause.) Mr. J. GXIFFITHS then proposed "The workmen of the firm" and Mr. TROW responded at some length. He spoke of the unanimity which had existed between the workmen and their masters, but, he said, they could not help disagree- ments occurring sometimes. When these disagreements did occur it was always best to act within reason. He thought that they, as workingmen, ought to choose a committee from amongst themselves to which they might submit questions of difference.

Mr. MALKIN and Mr. BOULD briefly supported the last speaker. Mr. Brims, in making the presentation, said he had a duty to perform for which he felt himself quite unequal. He thought that all the kind things that could be said had been said with respect to Mr. Morris's character, while the address and the presents which they saw before them would hardly need any comment from him. When he first knew Mr. Morris he was but a paddler in the iron works, and he had risen from the ranks of labour to the position which he now held by sheer perseverance, determination, and plod- ding, and he considered that the life of any man who had succeeded as Mr. Morris had done was a fit model for any young man who wished to rise. He hoped Mr. Morris would live long to test the quality ef the presents. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. S. WILKINSON, in supporting the last speaker, spoke of the esteem in which Mr. Morris is held by the workmen, and referred to the disastrous effects of strikes; but, he said, with Mr. Morris at the head of affairs he had no fears of a strike occurring among the workmen of Dallam forge. Mr. PZUCY, of Wigan, in the course of some remarks of a complimentary character, said that he had the pleasure of nominating their friend, Mr. Morris the other day, as a member of the Geological Society of London. Mr. CIIITCHLET, in presenting a very beautiful biscuit basket to Mrs. Morris, said it appeared be was the only one there who had to speak for tbe ladies that evening, but he was proud of the duty which he had to perform. (Applause.) He could say that there were worthy women in the country as well as worthy men. No doubt when their esteemed manager had gone home with an aching heart she had given I him her sympathy, and he hoped she would live long to enioY her present. (Applause.) " The health of Mr. and Mrs. Morris" was proposed by Mr. MILLINGTON. _He said it was nearly 40 years since Mr. Morrie and he were strangers. They were boys together in the same ironworks, and commenced their iron career together. (Laughter.) Mr. FIELDEoush said he bad known Mr. Morris for They had puddled together side by side, n s found him an intelligent workman. div.head: HARE ON TRADE TOKENS, SIGNS, &c.
div.p: THE HARE ON TRADE TOKENS, SIGNS, &c.

Sir,—The hare figures on the token of John Perris, in the I Strand, London, 166; also of Nicholas Warren, in Alders- ; gate. But Warren evidently made a cockney mistake,j thinking that harem, like rabbits, lived in warrens. (See I London Gacette, No. 368.) Another hare was the sign of Philip lianas, in Wa'brook, in 1682. (London Gazette, Sep- ' tember, 18-21, 1682.) But in this instance the author of "The history of Signboards" is sure the newspapers have wade a misprint. (Oh, these printers! No wonder composi- tors are jocularly nicknamed "donkeys," and pressmen "pigs." It is also a curious fact that both the biped disciples of Caxton and the quadrupeds named are certainly connected with "marks ;" but as regards the latter what a difference there is in the connection—the one a blessed impress; the other a satanic pinch.) "I am confi- dent," says Mr. Larwood, "that the man's name was Haase, the Dutch or German equivalent for the hare he represented on his sign." Talking of transpositions or corruptions, a case has just come under my notice where "pot-house poli- ticians" comes out as " pothouse publicans; while in another case the substitution of an r for a c in a sentence naakesit appear as If a cow could bark. Perhaps the editor may one of these days feel inclined to grant me a short space to describe some peculiarities and curiosities in connection with "paper-staining." However, it is worthy of mention to the credit of printers, that Mr. Larwood's book does not record a single instance of a public-house sign that can boast a direct connection with the Caxtonian art. Though the "Hare and Hounds" often figure to- gether on the signboard of Boniface, it only appears twice in that capacity in connection with other animals, and these are the squirrel and the cat. So it would seem that there is warrant for, and point in, Mr. Bartlett's remark that it would require a cat without a tail and a rabbit with along tail to prove the possibility of producing a hybrid between the feline and the rodent species. The sign of the "Hare and Squirrel," I believe, is to be found at Nunheaton, that of the "Hare and Cat" at Norwich. The French have a pro- verb the English equivalent of which is, "He beat the bush, another caught the hare ;" and yet in France the skin of that rodent is not so highly valued, as a fur product, as it might be. Another French proverb is to the effect that "the hare 'Comes to die in its form "—" Le lievre revient toujours eon fate." A third says "hares cannot be caught by beat of drum." In fact, the hare and the method of its pursuit in some form or other pervades our literature. It and the hound appear in person, symbol, or simile, but as a rule always in connection with legitimate sport, the pointing of a moral, or the adorning of a tale. In "Ovid's Metamorphoses," Cephalus thus describes the action of the celebrated hound Procris presented him with after their re-union, when he releases it from the leash to attack the ravenous beast that is decimating the flocks and herds of the shepherds of Aonian Thebes:—

"Nor straight he fled Across the plain, but still with shifting course, By instinct taught, the too impetuous foe In rapid doubles baffling." The hound is the natural enemy of the Bare, and the Creator has endowed each and both of them with the in- stinct to avoid and to attempt to baffle the other. What a needless perfection of cruelty it seems to me to attempt to artificially propagate and extend those instincts by a class of persons who profess to derive gratification and enjoy- ment from a periodic indulgence in so-called sport. The hare wrests no tithe from them against their will. Hence they have no right or warrant to deprive it of it life or liberty in the way of a public exhibition. With this letter I wil leave the subject of "coursing" to the serious atten- tion of readers of The Exansiner, thanking the editor once more for his courtesy, and hoping thatl have not offended the sense or feeling of anyone, “ Newtonian " •more especially.—l am, air, &c., ANGLO-SCOTUS. _ _

, Newington, London. P.S.—I had almost forgotten to mention that, in case any Newtonian, while taking his walks abroad, should be in- vited by a clergyman, during Lent or on a fast day, to step into the parsonage and have a bit of something to eat, and be asked by the cleric to sit down and partake with him of what looks like roast hare and perk chops, the guest must not rashly assume that the viands are such. In all proba- bility the one dish will be St. Patrick's trout, and the other a roast otter, the flesh of this animal having been admitted by authority to be maigre—i.e., food fit for a fast day. Pro- perly dressed, it looks very like roast hare.—A.-S.

There was once pris_s offered for the best essay on the influence of machinery on art 'prosperity of the people, anti Mr. Morris took the first peae. When he left Mr.Thorneycroft'er—where he had been manager, to come to Warrington—the work- men shuwed their esteem for him by presenting him with a grand tegimonial. But the testimonial they were now going to give him was even better than any he lrad had before.

Mr. SIMPSON and Mr. SMITH also supported. MT. MORRIS, in acknowledging the gift, said rhen a few days ago he heard of the efforts made to present him with a testimonial, a feeling a satisfaction amounting almost to eentacy ran through his system. The very many nice things that had been said of him •hadi been like pouring cold water down his back. With all this heart and soul he thanked them for that expression of feeling towards himself and wife. He could assure them that the words were ten thousand times more to him than the actual presents which would fade some day. The words they had said would never fade away from his memory, and he hoped they would have an effect upon the 'young men, not only in that room, but to the young men at Bewsey and Dallam Forges and at Wigan also, and in fact in other towns. With regard to the provident societies and the agreement about the Liability Act, he could say that he knew if they could get an understanding between their employers and men they would live in harmony and good feeling towards each other; and if at any time an accident might take place, he felt that the thing would be amply compensated, and the donor and recipieot be content. They had had sufficient coblinOß sense to form their own insurance society. He enquired from one of the agents of a society a short time ago how much he would want for ironworkers supposing they insured in his society. On being told what they paid in wages he said they would want £750 a year. By this transaction the men, by having their own association, saved £BOO all the money paid by them and to them ; not a fraction went anywhere else. So that they were a sort of happy family in this par- ticular instance. Nothing pleased him better than seeing young men treading in the same path he did 26 years ago. hen he studied chemistry they had a very bad rnauipul- /nor, and they had often to subscribe whenever be broke a costly piece of glass, which was very often. It was very hard times for him. He exhorted the young men to take advantage of every means of improvement. (Applause.) He hoped to continue-so long as he was with them to merit the same good feeling that had been so much displayed that evening. (Applause,) The CHAIRMAN proposed "The visitors," and coupled with it the name of Mr. Robinson.

Jigtice Day passed sentence of five years' penal servitude on Thomas Alexander H eyes Robinson, of Mount Orrell, near Wigan, a person of some wealth, who, in resistance to an attempt to arrest him which was being made under an order of the Court of Chancery, discharged firearms in a most reckless manner. The Judge told the prisoner—what must have been apparent to anyone who read the remarkable story told at the trial— that the jury had taken an indulgent view of his conduct in convicting him under one of the minor counts of the indict- ment, and His Lordship refused in emphatic language to make any distinction between this "gentleman " and an ordinary criminal.

RAINHILL. FAILING TO RITPORT A CASICs ow SWINIII FEVER.— Patrick Farrell, of Rainhill, was charged at Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. W. L. Evans (in the chair), A. R. Gladstone, Willis, and Gibbon, with having had a case of swine fever and not reporting the same to the police.—lt appeared that on the 12th instant, a police- constable stationed at Rainhill, in consequence of informa- tion which he had received, went to the defendant's house and asked him if he had killed a pig that morning. The defendant replied that he had, and showed him a pig which was hung in the back kitchen, dressed as if intended for human food. The pig was fat, but only about half grown. The officer asked him how long the pig had been ill, and the defendant replied that it had not been ill at all ; it was all right on the previous night, and he had got a man named Howard to kill it that morning, and when it was opened they found a hot potato in its throat. The officer told the defendant that he should report the case to Superintendent Barker, and defendant then asked the officer to let him know ;he result as soon as he could, because he intended going to St. Helens that morning to see about selling the pig. The officer reported the case to Superintendent Barker and returned to the defendant's, but could not see him until nearly eleven o'clock at night, when he told him he must not remove the pig until it had been inspected by Superintendent Barker and Mr. Welaby. The summons was served on the 18th, and on Sunday, the 19th inst., defendant met the offiaer and said, "What are you going to do with me about this pig? It is no use me telling any lies about it; I found it dead in the cote that morning, and I got Howard to come and dress it." —Jaraes Welsby states that he examined the pig, and found that it had been suffering from swine fever, and must have been ill at least two days.—The defendant was fined 10s. and costs, £2 is. ad.

Assam:llmi i CONSTASLE.—James Taylor and Richard Evans were charged, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tues- day, with assaulting P.C. Kaye on the 16th alt.—The officer stated that his attention was called to a disturbance at Whiston. He went to the place in plain clothes and found some men fighting. He struck a match, the night being very dark, and saw the two defendants, who, as soon as the light went out, commenced to assault him. Taylor kicked him and Evans struck him with his hand, after which they' ran away. He had no doubt as to the identity of the defen- danta.—Bvans was ordered to pay lOs and costs, and Taylor, who had been before the Bench this year for poaehing, was ordered to pay 405 and costs.

. - ASSAULTING A POLICEMAN WITH A. HATCHET AT Wnis- ToN.—Samuel Tittler, was charged at Prescot Petty Ses- sions on Tuesday, before Messrs.W. L. Evans (in the chair), Gladatene, Willis, and Gibbon, with assaulting P.C. Kaye, at Whiston, on the evening of the 11th Kaye said he was on duty near Platt Bridge on the night in question, and heard a disturbance at some distance. He went to the place and there found the prisoner's wife, who was drunk. Before he could speak to her she went into the house, and he followed her to tell her that he would report her for being drunk and disorderly. As soon as he got in- to the house, the prisoner, who was sitting on a chair at the opposite side of the room, got up, rushed to the bottom of the stairs, picked up the hatchet produced, and ran across the floor, and struck him a blow on the chest, and gave him a violent kick on the ankle. He fell, and could not rise because of the pain from his ankle. He crawled aoross the yard, and was raising himself by means of some rail- ings, when the prisoner hit him on the right side of the head with the lhatchet, causing a wound, from which he lost a great quantity of blood. He then struck the prisoner with his truncheon, and knocked him to the ground. The prisoner got up and went into the house, aud he followed him and took him into custody. The prisoner resisted, and struck him on the head, face, and body, and he had to obtain assist- ance, after which the prisoner went quietly. He had since been attended by Dr. Hall.—Dr. Hall said when the last witness came to his surgery he found a lacerated wound on the scalp extending. over an inch in length, which might have been caused by a blow from a blunt instrument, such as the hammer end of the hatchet produced. He had sin& had his atteation called to the officer's ankle, and found a large contused swelling.—The prisoner was committed to the quarter sessions for trial.

MUSICAL ETNNING.—The third of the musical evenings set on foot to provide funds for a Christmas dinner for the poor of Over and Wharton came off in the Board School, High-street, on Monday last. The Rev. G. W. Ninis, vicar of St. Chad's, presided. The programme, as usual, consisted of instrumental pieces by Mr. Vernon's string band, which were well rendered; songs by Miss Woodvatt (accompanied by Mrs. Woodyatt on the piano and the Rev. E. Woodyatt on the violin), Miss Peck (encore), Mr. F. B. Cooke, Mr. Fletcher (Northwich), both encored. Two piccolo solos by Mr. Hughes, of Northwich, were very much appreciated. Mr. T. Kennerley, whose excellent playing is well known, gave "Home, sweet home," on the cornet. There was also a recitation by Mr. F. H. Cooke and a readtng by Mr. Ellison. Mr. Singleton presided at the piano. The audience was not very large, awing to the inclement night. , SUDDIIIN DII&TH.—On Sunday last, a woman named Jane Robinson was found dead in her room. She lived alone, and kept a small shop in High-street. She was last seen alive late on Saturday night. A neighbour knocked at her door on Sunday about dinner time, but receiving no reply she went away. On returning again at two with the same result a policeman was fetched, who got in at the window and found her dead in her bedroom. Her death must hare occurred during the night, as she was in her night dress. CHI3IICII OF ENGLAND TBMPBRANCII SOCINTY.—The Church of England Temperance Society held a meeting in the Town Hall, on Wednesday night last, when W. H. Yerden, Esq., J.P., occupied the chair. There were support- ing him on the platform Dr. Bullock, of Canada,. chaplain to Her Majesty's forces there; also the Rev. C. Can vicar of Wharton; Rev. W. H. Hopkins, M.A., vicar of Moulton; the Rev. G. Wyatt Ninii, vicar of St. Chad's; with Dr. H. Leak and J. Hewitt, Esq. The attendance wae excellent, considering the state of the weather.—The speech of the chairman gave a good tone to the undertaking, as was likely, when we find that he is ready to join with those who press to the force the grand subject of temperance as the handmaid of religion.—Dr. Bullock, who was well received, spoke with no uncertain sound. He has only one remedy for the evils of intemperance—total abstinence. Ile used to feel proud that we had such a number in the army, but he now thinks that the vast army of railway employs- -350,000—in our country is in advance of it in the matter of temperance, for while 1-30th are on account of drunkenness punished in the army, there is three per cent, only dismissed from the railway service annually. He spoke hopefully of the near approach of the time when the evil shall be banished from the churchos and homes of England. He looked on all such workers, whether Good Tempters, Sons of Temperance, Recbabites, Blue Ribbonites, or whatever they might be called, as so many workers for the Saviour, and the rescue of precioas souls.—The customary compli- ments closed the proceedings.

THE EMPRESS OF AUSTRIA'S VISIT TO CHESHIRE.—The gratifying intelligence has reached Cheshire sportsmen that the Empress of Austria is about to revisit Cheshire during the hunting season, and will again take up her residence at Combermere Abbey. Her Majesty is expected early in January. She will be accompanied as before by Prince Rudolf Leichtenstein. Several of her Majesty's hunters have already arrived at Combermere, and are being kept in training with the Cheshire hounds. CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.—The adjourned Quarter Sessions for the county of Chester was held an Tuesday, at Knutsford ; Mr. Horatio Lloyd (the deputy chairman) pre- sidiag. In charging the grand jury, the Deputy Chairman said the calendar contained the names of 29 prisoners, as against 33 this time last year. Amongst them were two cases of unlawful wounding and one of malicious damage; the rest were eases of larceny. The number for trial in- I eluded a large proportion of old offenders, 16 out of the 29 having been previously convicted.—Ciroi/ Business: The Chief Constable reported that since the last Quarter Sessions in October eleven animals had been attacked with pleuro- pneumonia at Bridge Trafford, near Chester. Swine fever had appeared in eight places, and sheep scab existed on four farms. The register of the milk trade had been revised, and the number purveying milk in the county was now registered as 2,715, there having been a gradual decrease since 1879, when the number was 3,314. CHARGE OF FORGERY AGAINST A SCHOOLMASTER.— Henry Seymour, late of the British Schools, Tarporley, was charged on Saturday, at Tarporley, with forging a cheque for £25. Prisoner left Tarporley in October, and returning in the middle of the following week, he found his situation had been filled by the managers. Prisoner remained unen- gaged for about a month, when Mr. Wright, secretary of the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association, gave him some temporary employment is connection with the recent dairy show at Chester. In this way, Mr. Wright stated, he assumed the prisoner obtained possession of his cheque book, as it was missing about this time. On Tuesday last the prisoner presented at the Old Bank, Chester, a cheque drawn on the account of the Dairy Farmers' Association, and signed by three members of the committee in favour of Mr. Wright, secretary, for £25, and the money was paid over to him. On Friday the bank book was returned te Mr. Wright, who then ascertained that a forgery had been committed, and suspect- ing the prisoner, caused him to be arrested. A clerk from the bank was telegraphed for, and oa arriving be identified the prisoner as the person who drew the money. Evi- dence to this effect haying been given, the prisoner was remanded until Wednesday, when he was committed to the Assizes for trial.

CONYERBNCE OF CruEratnn CRICLPITHRS.—A meeting of Cheshire cricketers was held at Crewe on Saturday; repre- sentatives from Chester, Birkenhead, Stockport, Rock Ferry, Macclesfield, Northwich, and other places attending. The Rev. W. Armitstead, of Goosetrey, presided, and Mr. A N. Hornby was in the vice-chair. Both the Chairman and Major Dixon urged the necessity of leaving a thoroughly good and representative cricket club for the country. Such a club once existed in Cheshire, but of late years there had been considerable difficulty in getting together a sufficient number of good players. Some of the best local clubs belonged to towns situate on the borders of the country—Birkenhead, Stockport, Chester, Sale, and Crewe. The County Club had an excellent ground at Chelford, but the place did not seem sufficiently central.—Mr. James Horner, Stockport, slid that a number of gentlemen of Chelford had used the term "Cheshire County Cricket Club," but he understood there was really no county club in existence. He therefore pro- posed that a fresh County Club should be started, and that each local club which desired to join should be entitled to have an equal number of representatives on the committee. —Mr. Hornby proposed that the club should have a central ground at Crewe.—After some discussion, it was decided to form a new County Club, and to invite local associations to send representatives.
At the Cheshire adjourned Quarter Sessions, on Wednes- day, Mary Cox, 29, servant, for stealing £2 10s. and a purse from Griffiths Roberts, at Runcorn, was sentenced .to four mouths' bard labour.

BAPTIST CHAPEL arNIVERSARY AT EARLESTOWN. The anniversary sermons in connection with the Earles- town Baptist Chapel were preached on Sunday last by the Rey. S. Havvkes, of Liverpool, Both morning and evening there was a large and atte:tative congregation, who listened with great interest to tb.4 preaching of the rev. gentleman. Collections were =drain aid of the chapel debt fund. Tho sum of £7 2s. 6d. 'etas realised The annual -.fleeting was held in the chapel on Monday evening, wten about 200 persons sat down to a substantial tea. The chair was afterwards occupied by the Rev. W. C. Taylehe pastor, and he was supported by the Rev. Mr. Moore (Warrington), and Mr. E. J. Weaver (Earlestown). , The CHAIRMAN, in his introductory remarks, said: It is now my duty to call upon our secretary (Mr. Aveline) to I give a report of the past year—of the first year really of our being in this place of worship. It is now somewhere about twelve months since we entered into this place, and during that twelve months I believe that we have been working with the blessing of God resting upon the work. The sec- retary will now give us his report. Mr. ATELINR then gave a lengthy address. With respect to a report of what had been done he had nothing very special to mention. They had not made any great progress I —in fact during the year they had been undertaking more , particularly the work of consolidation, (hear, hear) settling down, oiling the machinery, and getting generally into working oder. As they had now got into that position, doubtless with the blessing of God, at that time 12 months hence they might have to report some substantial progress. When they came into their chapel their membership—that was the number of persons who had put on Christ by bap- tism, was 41. During that year there had been added by profession, 2; by transfer from another church, 1; and by baptism, 6; total, 9 ;—(hear, hear)—making their member- ship 50. But they had lost by transfer to other churches 2, so that their membership was now 48, or a gain of 7 during the year. (Applause.) With respect to the Sunday school, that work had been steadily carried on, although no very great advancement had been made. Yet, the status quo had been kept and retained, and more even than that. At the commencement of the year they had 200 members of the Sunday school, but now they had 215. He was very glad to he able to report that the children attended very regularly, and that their school registers were kept in such a manner as to correctly represent the state of the school. The children were divided into classes, and were taught by 14 teachers. With respect to their congregation, they had most certainly improved. When they were in the Co-operative Hall they had not usually more than 100 persons at the evening service. If they had that number the room seemed to look pretty full, but as a rule they now had 159—(hear, hear)t—so that they had certainly been making progress in that direction. They were glad to con- tinually see strange faces—although that fact might cut both ways. It might be deduced from it that people were disgusted with them, and turned in somewhere else, but he did not think that was the case. There was no doubt that if all the members of their congregation could be got together at one time there would be nearer 200 than 160. In connection with their church they had a mothers' meeting—and he mentioned it first because it was one of the most important and because it was on the first day of the week. It was looked after and directed by their worthy sister, Mrs. Street, who had given to the meetings a good deal of her attention and care. Doubtless there would be great good arising from them. He had full authority to invite any ladies to attend that meeting, for that was one of the ways in which they could help, and thus be the means of blessing not only that church but the neighbourhood at large. On the Monday evening they had a prayer meeting which had been very well attended by a good many young people who seemed to take great interest in it. It might be a great deal better attended, though it varied considerably; they had had as many as 25 and 26, while it had been as low as 15 many a time. In connection with their church they also had a temperance branch—(hear, hear)— that took the form of a Band of Hope and Gospel temperance service. (Hear, hear.) They were not a tem- perance church, and it was not incumbent upon all who joined them that they should be total abstainers, but he would like it to be known in the neighbourhood that tem- perance was part of their church work, and ho hoped the time would never come when it would be disregarded or thought little of. Doubtless the Blue Ribbon Army and other temperance organisations were doing a good work, but he was firmly convinced that if total abstinence was to spread, and to become permanent in the land, churches would have to take it up and make it part of their work. The membership of their Band of Hope had increased since they came into the chapel from 65 to 124. Meetings were held for the children every Tuesday evening at seven, o'clock, while every fortnight they had meetings for the adults. He thought there were somewhere about 50 or 60 upwards of 15 years of age who were connected with that senior branch of the Band of Hope, but they would like to see those num- bers swell considerably. Then they had a noble band of tract distributors. There were 20 distributors, and they visited 650 houses weekly. It was a work which had accomplished much in the past, and they hoped it would be carried on in such a manner that great good would come from it in the future. It was more particularly under the direction of their brother Mr. Howard, who gave a great deal of attention to it, and who brought his organising ability to bear upon it, and it at present was in a very good position. During the year ending 30th September last there had been raised by the Earlestown congregation in that place by weekly offerings and pew rents—they had had no collections-105 14s. lid. They had received from their friends at Liverpool £l5, and from , the Baptist Association £l5, so that their total income had I been £135 14s. 101 They had expended £135 14s. 10d., I so that they would soon see how much money they had in hand. With respect to the Sunday school they had a separate account. By their collections in August last they raised £l9, which was £5 more than they ever raised before. They bad paid all liabilities, and had a sum of £8 or £9 in hand. In connection with the chapel they had an awkward, ugly thing—a debt—to deal with. It was £450 when they came into the chapel, but they-bad received £2OO from the Baptist Building Fund, which they had to pay back in ten years by half-yearly instalments of £lO, free from interest. They had paid two half-yearly instalments, thus leaving their debt £430. They had £250 borrowed on interest at the rate of five per cent., which meant £l2 108. per annum to be paid. It was an awkward charge—one they did not like, and one they would be glad to get rid of. It was towards that debt that the collections on the previous day and the proceeds of that tea party were being devoted. They hoped to get £lO clear by those services, and then by striving futther they would soon be able to wipe off the ugly incumbrance of £250 (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN thought the report was one for which they had c muse to be deeply thankful, and these who had been banded together and had entered into the various works had great reason for encouragement. As they looked at the past year they could find encouragement to do mere than they had done, and to enter more earnestly and more sincerely into the work. (Applause.) The Rev. Mr. MOORIC, of Warrington, expressed his pleasure at being present, and having the opportunity of viewing that beautiful little chapel—a perfect gem—which created within him feelings of envy. He was glad to hear that the work was going on se nicely, and was certain that they had got a most indefatigable and useful secretary. rhe report showed a year of good, steady, solid work. He urged upon them that they should not allow any of the works in I connection with that church to go down for lack of sup- port. He believed in a working church, and be believed ' that there was something for them all to do. Christian love was one of the very first and important elements of success, and they should give any " strangers" a hearty and sincere welcome. Everyone could pray—and that was a necessity—while everybody could work by living a holy life, for by a coneistent and holy life they recommended the religion of Jesus Chrigt to all with whom they came in contact. He thought there was a tendency in the pulpit preaching of the present day to obscure and overlook the great truths of the Gospel which had been honoured in all times by the Holy Spirit to the conversion of men and the building up of His church. He thought there was a tendency in much of the public thought to overlook that great cardinal and important doctrine, which he thought was the true pillar, basis, and foundation of the whole structure of Christianity, and that was the abso- lute necessity of all atonement for sin. He thought there was no other thing in the universe that could save men but that, and when a church of Christ obscured or reketed that great truth, as it was rejected at the present day, he thought that ruin was not very far off. He alluded at some length to the drink tralUe as the greatest enemy they had to con- tend against, and he said it could only be successfully coped with by the united strength and persistent opposition of the church of Jesus Christ. He encouraged them to continue their good work, and not be discouraged if they did not see great results. (Applause.) Mr. E. J. WRAVRR then gave an earnest address dealing principally with the temperance question. He observed that he had been watching their labours for the past seven years, and he congratulated them upon the measure of success that had attended them. They must not despise the day of small things, for they found that most of the great works that had been accomplished in the world had had small beginnings. Though they had a small beginning in Earlestown they had now one of the first places in the town. If they did not take the first place for congregation, or in the number of those who attended, he thought they took the first place for the beautiful building they had to wor- ship in. He was pleased that they had got almost all the organisations at work which it was possible to have con- nected with a church, and he would say" go on and prosper in the name of the Lord." The Band of Hope movement was a grand thing, for they were gathering in the boys and girls who would be the fathers and mothers of the future. They were working for the future as well as for to-day. They did not always see the result in the present day— they had to now in hope, and sometimes they had to sow in tears. They wanted their country to become sober, and then it would become free, for the drinking :customs enthralled it and made its name a by-word amongst other nations. They must themselves prepare for the future, and he hoped that when the summons came they might all have the "well done" of the Master. (Applause.) In a very atde address, Mr. ASHTON moved a hearty vote of thanks to the ladies who had contributed their services, and also to the choir and harmoniumist (Mr. Eckersley).— Mr. Comae seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation. During the evening the choir was conducted by Mr. Aveline, and excellently gave two anthems. Mr. Holds- worth sung "No night there," whilst Mr. Ashton was en- coursed for singing "Why are you wandering here, 1 pray?" , He afterwards gave "Night is a river" in good style. Miss Lirnond and Miss Jackson were much appreciated for the duet. "A sea of glass."

div.p: EXAIBIT [ON OF GAS APPLUNCES • AT RUNCORN. It is to the credit of the Runcorn Gls Company that tiatv have been amongst the first to demcnetrate to the public en anything like an extensive scale the various Imes, outside that of lighting, to which gas can be applied for househeld purposes 'The increased interest witk which the electric light Wals regarded a year or two ago, when it was first -seriously put forward as a rival to gas, was accompanied by a no Ites intense interest in the established illuminater. The tiled was that efforts were strenuously made to utilize to a greater extent the powers of gas, and so active have been 'the parties concerned in constructing appliances to obtain this end that they are now very numerous. An exhibition cof these appliances, promoted by the Gas Company, was 'held in Bethesda schoolroom on Monday, and each day dur- ing the week. There is no doetbt that a great deal of pre- judice exists against using gas for any ocher purpose than that of lighting. The eechibition, in full operation, of appliances of every description is calculated in a great degree to remove this feeling, and the collection which was shown by the Gas Company was of a very representative character. One could not help noticing the neatness and compactness of the stoves on view. Their arrangement, too, was in all cases very simple, and the method of working equally easy. It is claimed for them that they are less dirty, more economical, and raore conve- nient in use than the ordinary coal fire. The claim of cleanliness most certainly cannot be withheld. Scientific authorities state that the smoke from the fires of our dwell- ing-houses is one of the chief, if not the greatest, polluter of the atmosphere, against the impurity of wnich great out- cries are sometimes raised. Gas fires seem to be practically smokeless, and their adoption in place of coal fires would appear to offer at all events a partial remedy for this grievance. Some of the stoves were constructed so as to carry on a great number of cooking operations at the same time, to be used in place of an ordinary cooking range, whilst others were only intended to supplement the usual household arrangement. One of the latter kind shown by Messrs. John Wright and Co., Essex Works, Birmingham, wastermed the "workingman's stove." It was a combined cooking and heating stove, and was priced at 21s. It was -supplied with one burner, and in eight minutes a quart of water could be boiled, a chop or steak cooked, and two or three•plecee of bread toasted. One pennyworth of gas was tatacient to cook six breakfasts. With another stove of a larger pattern it was stated that twenty pounds of meat ,otrald'be cooked for the expenditure of a penny in gas. A good selection of cooking stoves of a somewhat similar 'character was shown by Mr. Charles Wilson, Carlton Works, Leeds.; the stoves for heating purposes were numerous and of pretty designs. In some 'the heat was thrown into the room by copper reflectors, in Arthers a bunsen, or atmospheric gas flame, played upon asbestos or'platinum, which, immediately a light was applied to the gas, assumed the bright, cheerful appearance of a fire. The "cosey " tire, ter use in bedrooms, was a very neat arrangement. It could be kept alight at the small cost of id. per hour, and would warm a room fourteen or fifteen feet square. Mr. Fletcher, the well-known gas engineer, of Warrington, had also a number of exhibits, including a heating stove of a design which was much admired. He had also on view an in- genious" water heater." This was to be fixed to the water tap, and the gas lighted, when in a few seconds, a con- tinuous stream of hot water would be produced. Mr. Fletcher claimed special advantage for his cooking stoves, as did the other exhibitors. On entering the room the at- tention of the visitors was immediately arrested by a great variety of artistically treated globes and chandeliers, which were generally admired. Light was supplied to the former by Suggs' burners. It is important that we should state ' that the Gas Company is prepared te let the stoves out on hire at-a-small cost varying from a penny to threepence per week, with the option of purchase. -At the opening ceremony, which took place at 12 o'clock, there -was a large company present, who manifested great interest in the appliances. Mr. HIVES, the chairman of directors, in opening the ex- hibition, remarked that everything those present saw was purely practical, and the directors hoped they would I view it in that light. The directors were something like a " Cheap Jack "—everything they gave them was full value for their money. The object of the exhibition was to show that gas might be utilized for all manner of cooking, boiling, grilling and lighting purposes. They were aware that the gas com- panies of the country had become very apathetic. They were receiving their dividend and were quite content, and said very little to the public. But they had a paralytic stroke some time ago, and the doctors who were called in recommended that they should try galvanism. A spark of electricity came and set them all in motion, and he believed thatgas companies would benefit more by the energy electricity had infused into them than the directors of the electric lighting companies themselves. (Hear, hear.) At one O'clock luncheon, cooked entiNly by gas stoves fixed on the premises, was provided in the Public Hall, which had been decorated with plants from The Grange con- servatories. The stoves used were those of Messrs. Jno. Wright and Co., and Mr. Charles Wilson, and the many varieties of good which the menu included, from the haunch of venison to the delicate confection, were cooked to perfection, at a cost, for gas, of only 2s. Id. It was expected by many that the food would possess the un- pleasant flavour of gas, bet their expectations were happily net-realised—the various courses were not in the slightest degree "tinged." The manner in which the luncheon was cooked was justly regarded as a triumph for those who ad- yocated the use of gas, and that in the near future it will be more extensively utilized cannot be doubted. The names of the guests were :—Messrs. William Hayes (chairman), F. Rigby (vice-chairman), Jas. Handley, W. B. • Gibson. R. B. To ft, Wm. Whittaker, R. Forrester (directors); the Revs. Wm. Preston, M.A., J. D. Thomas' John Billing- ton, E. Williams; Messrs. J. 0. Jackson, John Simpson, 'Win. Handley, Geo. S. Hazlehurst, Dr. Steele, Robert Davies, Dr. MacDougall, E. Carey, Robert Shaw A. E. Fletcher (HM. inspector of Alkali Works), P. Shaw, J. J. -Speakman, G. J. Knight, E. A. Chorlton, Peter Briscoe, Lient.,Colonel Ashton, Dr. Mouritz, J. Carr (gas engineer, Widnes), F. S. Stevenson (gas engineer, Chester), F. A. Lake, James Pritchard, Dr. Mouritz, Thomas Norman, Jos. Williams, Henry Linaker (Frodsham), W. H. Linaker, W. Timmins, Geo. Rhodes, r. W. Salkeld, James Dobson, Wm. -Fisher, R. Lea, W. Brookes, Wm. Sutton. M. Barker, S. Taylor, and S. Pope. The .thia.ramax having proposed the usual loyal toasts, gave the "Army, navy, and volunteers," to which toast Lieutenant-Colons! ASHTON responded, remarking that he thought the army and navy bad in Egypt exhibited the same courage and daring as in the days of Wellington and Nelson. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN then proposed the "Clergy and minis- ters of all denominations," which was drunk with great cordiality. The Rev. W. PuesTow, in response, expressed his regret at the absence of the Rev. Canon Barclay, who was other- wise engaged, and said the clergy end ministers tried to do their duty. which sometimes was not a very pleasant one. They could not throw themselves in the van of scientific progress, but they could co-operate in scientific matters and associate themselves with scientific societies. They were glad to co-operate in enterprises such as that they were engaged in that day. He thought religion had nothing to 'fear from the progress of science. Instead of science being an opponent of the Christian religion, it was its 'great handmaid-, and the greater progress science made—especi- ally in geology—the more clearly it proved that the word of God was true. He was pleased at -the progress science had made so far as gas was concerned. The Rev. EVAN WILLIAMS also responded in a short -speech. The CRAIRMAN proposed "The town and trade of Run- corn." He was glad to see so many people connected with the town present. There were people who cavilled at their doings, but he was very much obliged to them for their attendance, and also to Dr. Steele, not only for the way in which he managed the town, bat for his presence there that day. (Applause.) The toast was duly honoured. Dr. STEELE, who was applauded on rising, responded, observing that he wished everything that was done to be done for the benefit of the town. Although he believed in electricity, he was sari that it could net have cooked such a dinner as they had bad that day. (Laughter and ap- plause.) The CHAIRMAN next gave the toast of " The Widnes Local Board," remarking that he was intimately connected with the town of Widnes, which he was delighted to see represented there that day. There was nothing antagonistic between Runcorn and Widnes in any sense—everything was congenial. (Hear, hear.) He was sure that if Widnes did anything worthy to emulate, Runcorn would not be slow to follow; while if Runcorn inaugurated any improvement, Widnes would be glad to follow them. The toast was drunk with warmth, and Mr. Carey was called upon to respond. Mr. CARRY said he was much obliged to the chairman for the way in which he had spoken of Widnes, and his kind- ness in coupling his (Mr. Carey's) name with the rising town. The people on the Widnes side of the river envied the Runcorn people their situation, their soil, their con- tiguity to the best part of the river ; they very much wished the river would flow on the Widnes side as it did on the Runcorn side; and they envied very much their power of hospitality, which they had that day witnessed. (Ap- plause.) They had enjoyed it, but he was afraid that the Local Board would not be able to return the hospitality because they laboured under the disadvantage of having to satisfy the claims of a Local Government Board auditor. He thought Runcorn had set an extremely good example to the neighbouring towns, in the way in which they had drawn Were be attention to the future of gas. (Hear, hear.)rs Trre in believed d .) He that the manufacture and the use of ga infancy. (Hear, hear.) The manufacture of gas, as Dr. Siemens had pointed out, might be developed to an enor- mous extent. Dr. Siemens proposed, as they no doubt knew, to divide coal gas into two parts—the strictly illuminating gas and the heating gas. Then he suggested that the coke should be consumed in our houses and manufactories, in place of coal. Electricity, in Mr. Carey's opinion, would probably be the illuminating power of the future, but he -thought that the possibilities of gas had been hitherto un- developed and were extremely great. They owed very much to the gas company for having shown them what could be done in the application of gas, and he felt they would all return to their homes with a determination to make use of the example set before them. (Applause.) In proposing the toast of the "town and trade of War- rington," with which was coupled the name of Mr. Robert Davies, the CHAIRMAN said he was very sorry he did not sin Mr. Patterson, of the Warrington Gas Company, pre- rent. He was a gentleman in whose conversation he (the

His name was a byeword for honourable conduct, and be (Dr. McDougall) could not help admiring the public spirit which had been displayed in bringing to a small plasse like Runcorn such useful instru- ments of cooking and heating as they had witnessed that 'day; and in providing the handsome banquet of which they had partaken in that room. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The toast was drunk with much enthusiasm. The Cerernerese, in reply, said he quite agreed that gas had a competitor in electricity, but if it had not been for electricity that exhibition would not have taken place. But gas companies were not in despair. They were perfectly satisfied with the profits they were making. He did not view electricity in antagonism. He thought instead of its being an injury to them that it would be a spur. The whole of their dinner that day had been cooked at a cost of 23. id, and although they might say they had suffered some incon- veniences through not having the stoves connected with a ' chimney, he thought if the dinner had been cooked by coal fires without a chimney they would not have been ;tile to get it at all. (Laughter and applause.) He (Mr. Hayes) was not one of the promoters of the Runcorn Gas Company. The late Mr. Rigby was one of the earliest promoters, and he was sorry he was not present that day. Gas and water companies should belong to the town and not to a body of private proprietors. He, did not know what he would de with the money if he got it, because investments were scarce; and although he did not want to part with his shares in the Gas Company. instinct told him, as a citizen of Runcorn, that these two companies should belong to the town. (Applause.) He knew that often a narrow spirit sprang up, but while be was a shareholder in the Runcorn Gas Company he would take care to see that what benefited the proprietors should also benefit the town of Runcorn. (Applause.) In concluding Mr. Hayes proposed "The health of the Vice-Chairman." The toast was received with much applause. Mr. RIGBY, in reply, referred to the business capacity and general courtesy of the chairman, to which was largely owing the success of the Gas Company. The Chairman brought the toast list to a close by proposing "The health of Mr. Frith, the manager of the Gas Company, and other officials." All commercial concerns unless well managed would not succeed. The Runcorn Gas Company had been most fortunate in having a gentleman who was not only thoroughly competent to manage the Gas Works, but was admitted to be an authority on the manufacture of gas. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with enthusiasm. Mr. FRITH, in responding, said his endeavours bad always been during the quarter of a century he had been the gas manager to do the best he could for his company, and at the same time to do the best for the gas consumer. (Ap- plause.)
AN UNANSWERED LETTER.

The CLERK read a letter addressed to the chairman from Mr. Hunter, who asked to be allowed to remind him the joint note to the Board signed by Messrs. Snoddy, Showan, and himself, dated August 12th, remained unlnswered. Father FINEGAN said the letter had been answered. The subject of the letter was discussed in committee, and rejected by the Board. A MEMBER remarked that perhaps no official letter had been sent to Mr. Hunter. Father FINEGAN said the clerk should have replied. He considered Mr. Hunter's method of procedure an inter- ference with himself and the committee. He thought he should have communicated with the clerk. • The CHAIRMAN said that was the rule. Father FINEGAN: It is the second time he has overridden the committee by writing to the chairman of the Board. I object most strongly to it. The letter was then referred to the Management Com- mittee, and the m eeting rose.

workingman's sons and daughters into competition with their own sons and daughters in the battle of life it must have been because of inherent Christien principle, which told the strong to help a7-...0 to give fair play. to the weak ;---to treat mry man as a brother, and every woman as a siste- - Came what I might of the competition. Let the bet re e -o .ne tue surface as cream rises to the top of the bo•II. Now-a-days every working man's children werre -..ea'Thcated in a thorough way, and if they showed wonerfo power they could rise until the air became too t}::tn and elevated for them to rise any further. And tteat was as it should be. If the middle and upper classee, having had the start, and still possessed the adventn,e, could not hold their own in a close competition, why they must blame themselves, and themselves only, for being passed in the race by others who deserved success, for success was only for the good and strong, in this impartial and discerning age in which we lived. He felt strongly that working people had a future before them, but he wished them to feel that they had a tangible present and make the best of it. And he 'knew of no better advice to give fathers , and mothers than this: Do what they could for their child- ren—it was the best spent money, time, energy, and sym- pathy—and by-and-bye their children would be their abun- dant reward—(hear, hear)—to say nothing of the higher reward of a good conscience before God and their neighbours. Speaking of teachers, the speaker said of all honourable callings he knew of none more self-denying or more honour- able than the calling of a teacher in an elementary school, and referring again to tke working classes, he observed that he believed increasingly in the working people. Only do justice to themselves and believe in the dignity of labour, and they would find sympathy enough and to i spare. He should soon have to cross the noblest structure in the world that splendid bridge that crossed the Mersey at Runcorn. The engineer who designed that must have been a man of power, of vast ability; those who paid for it were persons of substance and means; but those who disembowelled the iron ore from mother earth, who cast it into the hot burning furnace and saw it molten who drew it out and pressed it by the aid of machinery and modern science into well shaped metals, who rivetted it according to design into its present splendid form— were they to be counted of nought? were they to be forgotten for a single moment? No. The greatness of England depended upon its intellect, upon its pocket, and upon its honest labour. But these could do nothing but for the arm of the working people. (Applause.) If they wished to be prosperous and happy take care that the intellect had justice done to it, but take still greater care that the heart was moulded aright by the gracious influence of the spirit of God. He did not believe in man being made alone of flee!, blood, and brain power. All these he possessed, but he had a heart as well, and they must educate for long eternity afrthey must also educate for short and fleeting time. (Applause.) Mr. W. FISHER moved, and Mr. J. SALKELD seconded, a vote of thanks to Mr. Aspinall, which was accorded with great enthusiasm. The proceedings concluded in the ordinary way. ANNUAL DINNER.

he annual dinner of this club was held at the Central 'Hotel, Widnes, on Thursday evening, Mr. J. L. Muspratt presiding. The dinner, ef which about 50 persons partook, was served in an admirable manner, and did creditio Mr. Fowler, the caterer. The following gentlemen among others were present :—The Revs. G. Bond and S. Allen, Messrs. H. W. Deacon. J. A. Kirkpatrick (Adelaide, Australia), J. White, J. Matthews, T. D. Matthews, Sayce, Lewis, D. Forster, Kyle, Shenton, Lord, F. Young, Brown, Morland, Stone, Briggs, Burgess, W. Tilley, F. Simcock, F. Dibbs, W. Holt, and P. Price. After the usual loyal toasts had been honoured, Mr. KYLE read the report, from which it appeared that the first eleven had arranged for 18 matches, 4 af which ' were not played, 5 lost, and 5 drawn; against 5 won, 3 lost, and 6 drawn in the previous year. The second eleven arranged 17 matches, 7 of which were not played, 3 won, 5 lost, and 2 drawn; against 5 won, 3 lost, and 6 drawn in the previous year. This showed a falling-off in the general play of the club. The best bowling score had been made by Mr. C. H. Watson, who made 23.16 runs per innings, against the best score last year of 21.5 runs per innings. The second eleven best bat- ting average fell to Mr. R. Calland, who made 11.5 per in- nings, against that of 22 -of last year. The first eleven bowling list was headed by Mr. R. Moab, whose average was 10.10 runs per wicket, against the 6.38, the best average of last year. The best bowling average in the se- cond eleven was made by Mr. James Hough, who had handled 443 balls obtaining a wicket for every 6.71 runs made off his bowling, against 5 25 runs per wicket, the best average last year. The committee recommended that the prize bats be given to the above-named players. The juniors had played exceedingly well, having won 10 matches out of 14.
The CHAIRMAN said he.was sorry that none of those who bad won the bats were present to reesise them. The TREASURER (Mr.. Forster) regretted to hays

to report a deficit' which was mainly due to the various improvements which had been carried out. The subscriptions for the bowling green were £39 16s. 6d.' and the ordinary subscriptions £B9 ss. 9d., total £129 2s. 3d. The total payments amounted to £156 lie. 10d., showing a deficit of £29 9s. 10d., and adding to this £53 10s. as yet to be paid, there was a total deficit of £BO 19s. 78. There was, however, a sum of £33 outstanding sub- scriptions, which, after being deducted, would leave a deficit of £47 19s. 7d. To clear off this debt the members of ths club had been appealed to for special donations, and they had already received £5 ss. (Applause.) Dr. O'KEEFFE proposed the "Widnes Cricket Club, and the President." He said he had great pleasure in doing so, although he was not a member of the club. He should, however, join the club, and do what he could in the future to help it on. In coupling with the tout the name of Mr. Gossage, he said that gentleman, whesever he could do any good for the town, was always willing to do it. The toast was drunk with enthusiasm. The CM/LIBMAN, in responding, said when the name of Mr. Gossage was coupled with the toast he could not refrain getting up to drink it, although his own name was included. They would all know the reason why he had done that,—it was because the name if their old president, he might say their perpetual president— had been coupled with it. In referring to the defeats which the English cricketers had this season received at the hands of the Australians he said that we had certainly won some of the battles, and he was glad to say that they had got a gentleman there that evening who had done something towards it, and that was Mr. Briggs. (Applause.) The toast of "The officers of the club" was then proposed

by Mr. R. LEWIS. He said that no society could sueceed unless it was well officered. He was proud of the present officers of the Widnes Cricket Club, and he thought they all ought to thank them for the way in which they had kept up its credit. They were ornaments to the club, and not ornaments only, for whenever they were called upon for the sinews of war, then it was they would be found useful. As treasurer, they had their inestimable friend Mr. Forster —(hear, bear)—whose name was what might be called a "household word" in the Widnes Cricket Club, and whether the club was in debt or not, so long as he remained its trea- surer its credit would be kept up. They had now got a very good ground and a splendid bowling green, both of which were well fenced, and any gentleman could go on a Saturday afternoon and spend an hour very pleasantly indeed. Refer- ring to the deficit, he said that the club was always getting into debt, but it was always making strenuous efforts to get out of it, and so it went on. He mentioned the names of the secretaries, Mr. Deacon and Mr. Longton, and said that the fact of Mr. Deacon holding office in the Widnes Cricket Club was its tower and strength. Mr. DEACON responded, and in the course of his remarks he said that Mr. Forster had read a statement of accounts which showed a nett deficit of about £47, but Mr. Forster had received .£5 55., and he (Mr. Deacon) had no doubt bet that this would be increased to £l5 or £2O, thus leaving £27 against the clnb. Mr. White had promised to get up a concert, and the proceeds from this would still further lessen the deficit. The deficit this year had arisen really through the improvements that had been made in the grounds; but this, of course, would not have to be done next year, and he had no doubt that then the subscriptions would cover the expenses, and the club would be in a fair position. Mr. SPOONER gave "The Vice-Presidents," and said that the names of Major Cross and Mr. Carey were closely associated with anything that was for the good of Widnes. They had each materially heightened the state of manufac- turing industry in the tows!. It was good for the club that they had such men among them,:because it tended to increase and stimulate their interest in the game. The toast was heartily drunk, and Mr. CAREY responded. The "honorary members" was next proposed by Mr. WRITE, who was glad to say they bad obtained another honorary member during the last two or three minutes. Mr. Bond had just handed him his subscription. (Hear, hear.) He wished it to be known that the bowling green was not a drag on the club as some supposed, but actually assisted it. Mr. Marrimws responded. - - - _

Mr. KIRKPATRICK proposed "The town and trade of Widnes." He said that he belonged to Adelaide, Australia, but had come over to Englond for the benefit of his health, and he was staying at Mr. Deacon's. He did not know what Widnes was before he came, but they had now got some capital footpaths, good wide roads, etc., and it seemed to be a very well kept town. He was not a practical cricketer, but he took considerable interest in the game, and he was glad that their Australian cricketers had been so successful in England. (Applause.) He understood that the Widnes Cricket Club had not had an opportunity of playing against them. (Laughter.) He stated that he would be glad to forward through his freind, Mr. Deacon his subscription towards lessening the deficit. (Applause) Mr. CAREY responded at some length. He said he re- membered saying, in answer to a question by someone, that there was not much light for the success of the town of Widnes, but since then there had been two new works intro- duced into Widnes, for which they were very glad. Hitherto' they had had all their eggs in one basket—their interests had been in the alkali works under the old process. They had now got a new trade, and there was every probability that they would have more after a time. With respect to the athletic position of the town he did not think they had gone back at all. Their football club had been successful against one of the best teams in the district. Mr. CAREY proposed the "Widnes Athletic Club," which was responded to by Mr. Barlow, and the " Widnes Football Club," which was responded to by Mr. Deacon. The other toasts included" The Press "and "The Lanca- shire witches."
WIDNES AND RUINCORtI CANARY SOCIETY. ANNUAL _SHOW YESTERDAY.

The second annual show of this society was held in the Volunteer Hail, Widnes, yesterday; but the attendance of the public was not large, probably owing to the most un- propitious state of the weather. Although only formed about twelve months ago, the society gives encouraging signs of success, the entries for the show this year being 59 in excess of those of last year. It is under the patronage of Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., J.P., J. Brock, J.P., G. Pilkington, J.e., F. H. Gossage, J.P., C. W. Hazlehurst, J.P., J. P. Liddell, Major Cross, and Dr. Booth. Mr. S. Davies is chairman of the Committee of Management, and Mr. John Pickthall the secretary. The exhibition comprised 17 classes, and the prizes varied from 10s. to 25., while special prizes were offered to members of the society. In all the classes the birds were in the finest condition and of the brightest plumage,many of them having won prizes at exhibitions of note in the south of England. The judge was Mr. S. Williamson, of Nantwich, and he awarded the prizes as follows: Clear or ticked yellow Belgians: 4st (not awarded), 2nd Samuel Davies. 3rd Trevlyn and Wright, 4th and sth William Mottram, ' Clear or ticked buff Belgians: 1 and 3 Trevivn and Wright, 2 Samuel Davies, 4 William Mottram, 5 J, Aire, 6 Henry lihone.
Songs were given at intervals by Mr. W. Holt, Mr. White, Mr. Briggs, senr., and Mr. Briggs, junr., and others altogether a very enjoyable evening was spent.

THE " MACINETAIRE " IN WARRINGTON.--Mr. Lonsdale again announces that he is compelled to remain in this town for another week. We publish new local testimonials from grateful patients. In looking over our columns it will be seen that every class of complaint seems to give way before the power of magnetism, and that after every (Aber remedy has been tried. The names and addresses of those who are willing to publicly testify to the great benefit they have de- rived are given, and as the addresses are not miles away, but in our very midst, there can be no fear of deception; in fact, Mr. Lonsdale courts every publicity, and has some thousands of testimonials, many from influential men, which he is I willing to show to any inquirer. The fact of his remaining I so long in Warrington is a sufficient proof of his success, and we recommend all sufferers to call and satisfy thein- selves.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD,
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD,

The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Victoria-road, on Thursday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. T. S. Timmis. There were also present the Revs. Father Clarke, Father Fimegan, Messrs. H. W. Deacon, John Brock, J. H. Davies, Robert Shaw, R. Bradshaw, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: EDUCATIONAL STATISTICS.
div.p: EDUCATIONAL STATISTICS.

The minutes of the District Education Committee stated that 146 applications for payment of school fees had been made during the month of October, and fees were recom- mended to be paid in 123 cases. The committee had before them 260 persona for contravention of the Education Act. Thirty-four were taken before the magistrates and convicted, and three children were sent to industrial schools.—Mr. W. H. W. DEACON gave a report of the work of the committee during the past year. He remarked that the parents did not seem to care for paying the fine of 5s now imposed. They seemed to find it easier to pay the fine than to send their children to school. SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE. The minutes of the School Management Committee con- tained a recommendation of the managers of Warrington- road school, that the resignation of -Mrs. Harrison, care- taker, be accepted, and that John Birkenhead be appointed caretaker and cleaner, at a salary of Hs. per week with residence, taxes, water, coal and gas free; he to provide all materials and labour requisite for the thorough cleaning of the school, and to perform such other duties as the managers may direct; that Mr. Thomas Roughley be appointed assistant master, boys department, at a salary of £45; that Miss Annie Winn be appointed assistant mistress, girls department, at a salary of £35 per annum. The Com- mittee recommended that the fees to be paid to the Board for pupils attending the central classes of pupil teachers who are not in the service of the Board should be £2 per annum in advance. It was reported that the Simms Cross managers had let a room to the Sons of Thnnerance for four monthly meetings for the sum of 32a.; also that they had let a class-room for ten evenings for the purpose of a French class, for the sum of 13s. 4d.—The minutes were passed.

TENDERS. The Sites and Building Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. Jno. Buck be accepted for the rfpairs, Icc., at Simms' Cross and at West Bank schools; and that the ten- der of Messrs. Roberts Brothers be accepted for the repairs at Warrington-road schools. The minutes were passed on the =thin of Mr. Brock.

NEXT MEETING. On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. Roar. Suaw, it was decided to hold the next meeting of the Board on the 21st December. • CORPORAL PIMISHMNNT : IMPORTANT DECISION. Mr. H. WADE DIACON, in rising to propose the motion which stood in his name, said he had a very decided opinion upon the subject of corporal punishment, of which he had had some little experience but he wished to say only what was right and proper. The members of the District Educa- tion Committee, of which he was a member, were brought into more intimate relation with the matter than the other members of the Board, and he must confess that the complaints of corporal punishment had been increasing in number, and he had felt it necessary to bring forward his motion.
