div.head: TRINITY DAY SCHOOLS CONCERT, RUNCORN.
div.p: TRINITY DAY SCHOOLS CONCERT, RUNCORN.

The annual concert, at which the successful scholars at- tending this school receive their prizes and certificates. was held in Runcorn Public Hall, on Thursday evening, and as in former years, was a great success. The committee had succeeded in prevailing upon Mr. Clarke Aspinall, of Liverpool, whe is very popular in the district, to be present and perform the daty of presenting the prizes. The scholars occupied seats on the platform, the body of the hall and the gallery being crowded with an audience well disposed to be pleased. The Rev. Wm. Preston, M.A., vicar of Holy Trinity Church, presided. The progrananae opened with the school song, "Cold the blast may blow," which was sung by the scholars with good taste. A dialogue, which was rewarded with much applause, followed, and the scholars sang" Beautiful moonlight." Master Temple sang the song "Evangeline " with a humming accompaniment, and he was loudly applauded. "The fisher boy " and "The first cuckoo," were then sung by the choir in a manner which evinced careful training. The duet, "What are the wild waves saying," was sung by Miss Robinson and Master Owen, and they received an enthusiastic encore, to which they responded: Mr. Aspinall then distributed the prizes, and delivered an address. The second part of the programme included: School song. "Song of the gipsies: song and chorus, "Won't you buy my pretty flowers F" Miss Robin- son; chorus, "The echo chorus"; recitation; song and chorus, "Driven from horse," Master Owen; round, " The sun is sunk."

Mr. ASPINALL, who was warmly applauded on rising, delivered a lengthy address, in which, after referring to the pleasure he had in being present, he said he knew of nothing wkich we ought all to cultivate more than domestic love, comfort, and happiness in the homes of our working folk, and one of the chief items of home bliss—and there was no place like home—must ever be the affection which existed between parent and child, child and parent. Be they rich or poor they would find that there were no pleasures, no joys, no blessings so true, so real or fascinating as the pleasures of a well-ordered fire side. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He had learned in his time that God's blessings were more evenly and equally dispensed than many were disposed to allow; because if it were true that a cottage home might have within it all the elements of real happiness, then what more could a palace home have within itself? Riches and position did not necessarily mean domestic bliss, and so if the working people of England, who had to strive hard for what they got, could only manage to have well-ordered homes full of happiness, they after all would compare favourably in their position with the highest of the land. From some statistics which had been placed in his hands, the success of the scholars at Trinity schools had been higher, according to the estimate shown by the Government grant received than any other school, church, denominational or board, throughout the land. (Applause.) All honour to Trinity Church schools; all honour to every- body concerned. In view of meeting a natural require- ment in a town like Runcorn, the managers of Trinity schools had established in January last classes for boys whose parents desired to pay more for their educational career than was paid under the ordinary conditions of the elementary school. He hoped the classes would be thoroughly appreeiated, and that that department of the school would be as creditable and as successful as all the other departments of it undoubtedly were. If he had to choose between a board school and a denominational school, he would ordinarily, for there was no rule without ex- ception, choose the latter in preference to the former. (Ap- plause.) In his judgment a denominational school was more likely to meet an the requirements of parochial and family life by a larger amount of sympathetic teaching than they would get in a school absolutely under board man- agement. Beard school management must be more or less perfunctory, although perhaps very efficient as compared with the other. But lie thought the Elementary Education Act was not passed one moment sooner than it was absolutely necessary for the well-being of the nation. (Hear, hear.) They had a School Board in Runcorn, and he heard that the Rev. Canon Barclay was its chairman. (Applause.) He disliked beyond anything empty flattery. He thought it was an impertinence to those to whom it was paid, but he ventured to say, as his conscientious convic- tion, that any School Board presided over by the Rev. Canon Barclay would be efficiently conducted in every detail. (Applause.) He had not a word to say against School 1 Boards, but if this country could have gone on with volun- tary education with efficiency, it would have been better ; but, unfortunately, they lacked efficiency until the strong arm of the law backed them up. Compulsory education was the law of the land, and likely to be, and he hoped it would remain 80 for all time to come. An uneducated child would in the future have a bard battle, and they would all understand that there was a greater obligation now upon parents to see that their children were well taught than there was before, because if every man in the workshop worked with sharp tools, it stood to reason that one with 1 blunt ones would not make as much as his neighbour. (Ap- plause.) The battle of life became fiercer and fiercer every day, and it was the duty of parents to see that their children were in such a condition as to be able 1 to struggle on with some chance of success by- and-bye when they became men and women. It was a poor thing for parents in any rank of life to think little or nothing of their own flesh and blood and to let their children blunder on anyhow and anyway so that they bad no great trouble or expense in bringing them up. Thank God, there were not many parents of that sort. What duty ought to be more thankfully received of God as one of the highest blessings that could be conferred upon fathers and mothers, what more precious to them and to Him than that His and their sons and daughters should be so armed for the battle that when their turn was over, and their heads low, their children should flourish and prosper by being well taught, because their parents did their duty by them when they had the chance. Speaking of schools and our relation in regard to them, Mr. Aspinall said years before the Edu- cation Act the Church of England did an enormous amount of educational work. No doubt other denominations did their part. Yet thoughtful working people, aed he thought most working people were nowadays, would see that if the middle classes had been striving all these years to bring the

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
The Queen will hold a Council at Windsor, at one o'clock on Tuesday next. A keeper, named Seathorne, was shot by poachers at Stevenage, Herts, on Thursday night. His life is despaired of.

The Paris Mona eur publishes a Madrid telegram, stating that 30 Socialists have been arrested in Andalusia supposed to be connected with the Lyons Anarchists. During the last three days the Prince of Wales has had excellent sport on Lord Walsingham's Norfolk preserves, though the weather has been unfavourable. The visit of the royal party will end to-day. An inquest was held at tiedney, near Spalding, yesterday, on the body of a child, aged 2-1- years, named Wbitsea. The mother of the deceased child left it in the bedroom, and on returning found that it had reached a bottle of carbolic acid, and drank a quantity of it. A verdict of accidental death was returned.

RAIKES STUART 869
There is great excitement. ARREST OF PROFESSOR PALMER'S MURDERERS.

The Allgemeine Zeitung of Vienna publishes the fol- lowing intelligence from Suez:—The Sheikh Abut Sasih, who conducted the ill-fated Palmer expedition, and who had been hitherto searched for in vain, was found on the Bth inst. by a party of Bedouin fishermen. They came up with him while he was wandering about the Asiatic seashore. A reward having been offered for his arrest, they bound him hand and foot and took him to Suez to the British Consul, who handed him over to the governor of the town. Another of the assassins, who was com- mander of the Nahle Fort, situated about three days' Journey in the desert in the direction of Syria, is like- wise in custody. BRUTAL TREATMENT OF A CHILD. ATI'EMPT TO LYNCH THE PRISONER.

Yesterday morning, Hugh Gorman, 24 years of age, an Irish labourer, residing at Bury, was brought up at the Bury Police Court, on a charge of haying committed an aggravated assault on Sarah Mould, a little child five years of age. The child's mother and Gorman lived together as man and wife, and the child, who is the illegitimate daughter of the woman, has been regarded as an eyesore by Gorman, who had treated it for some time in a brutal manner. On Thursday morning Gorman struck the child with his clenched fist OD the side of the head, knocking the other4side of the head against a chair. The child's screams drew the attention of the neighbours to Gorman's treatment, and a policeman was sent for. He, however, found the door locked. Nothing was seen of Gorman until nine o'clock in the evening, when he ventured into the street. As soon as he was seen he was set upon by a mob, who would have severely handled him but for the intervention of the police, who with some difficulty succeeded in taking him to the police station. Prisoner was remanded.

div.head: SERIOUS COLLIERY ACCIDENT: TEN MEN INJURED.
div.p: SERIOUS COLLIERY ACCIDENT: TEN MEN INJURED.

An alarming accident happened at the Carleton Main Colliery, Barnsley, yesterday morning. The men were being let down the shaft, when the cage, containing the fourth batch, was driven violently against the pit bottom. The engineman seemed to have lost control of the engine. The ascending cage was forcibly hurled into the headgear, smashing a portion of it and breaking the engine-rope. The cage had a narrow escape of falling to the bottom. One man had his leg broken, and nine others were seriously injured. 11IILL BURN I' DOWN NE -IR ASHTON.

Yesterday morning the Hazlehurst Cotton Mill, near Ashton-under-Lyne, was destroyed by fire. It was owned by a Radcliffa Limited Company, and contained 12,000 spindles. The fire was caused by friction in the machinery, land the flames spread with great rapidity, the roof falling in in less than an hour. - The damage is estimated at £lO,OOO. One man got badly hurt, and some of the work- people lost their property in their hurry to escape. A company of soldiers assisted in trying to extinguish the fire.

div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT,
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

H.M S. LIVELY.—MT. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN said it was a fact that H.M.S. Lively, on a voyage from Harwich to Sheerness, passed a vessel on shore on the Gunfleet Sands. The Lively had no lifeboats aboard, and the sea was running too high to communicate with the stranded ship. The Admiialty approved of the course the Lively took in pushing on for Sheerness, and telegraphing to Har- wich for the lifeboat to proceed to the ship's assistance. THE CUBAN REFUGEES—Sir C. DILKE said the British Government would not pledge itself to any course respect- ing the Cuban refugees until the report of the Committee of Inquiry had been received. PEERS AND ELECTIONS.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL said it was an infringement of the law for peers of the realm to vote at elections for members of Parliament, and such votes might he struck off on scrutiny. THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION: THE COST OF THE EXPEDI- TION.—Sir C. Duatn, replying to Mr. Errington, said there was no foundation for the statement in the Moniteur that Italy had taken the initiative in proposing a Conference on the Egyptian Question. Mr. GLADSTONE re- plying to Colonel Stanley, said that on Monday he would make a short statement on the cost of the military opera- tions in Egypt. He could not say whether an additional vote of credit or supplementary estimates would be asked for, but neither would be proposed during the present session. —The PREMIER told Sir W. Lawson he could not give him a day for discussing the subject of our military operations in Egypt. The motion was a vote of censure, and it was better such should be submitted when the House met next session.—Replying to Mr. Bourke, Mr. GL ADSIONEI said no conference had been proposed on Egyptian affairs.

Im- ports into Liverpool have been Email of wheat. Insignificant of maize, large of flour, and liberal of beans and peas. THE 'SECOND COMING OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST AT HAND.-The LECTURES on the above sub - ject, by an Evangelist serving under the L,rd's Restored Apostles, will be continued in the PUBLIC HALL, RUNCORN, as follows NEXT. NOVEMBER 29, The Restoration of Israel, and the completion of the work of Redemption.— Timmy, DECEMBER s—Antichrist: His rise, reign, and fall. —TUESDAY. DECEMBER 12—Babylon: What it is, and what is to become of it—TUESDAY, DECEMBER 19—Information con- cerning the work now doing utu'er Apostles in the midst of the Church universal; and evidence to satisfy Christians that it is not of man, but of God. Doors open at 7'30; Lecture to com- mence at 8. Christian people of every Denomination are earnestly invited to attend. All seats free.
